World.title: 10 books, 9 films and 8 songs about eclipses
World.content:
Since Antiquity, eclipses have been interpreted as omens, as punishment or as romantic metaphors, and that fascination has left its mark on literature, cinema and music. In fact, the phenomenon has been depicted in numerous paintings, but how have eclipses influenced the most popular artistic creations?

 

Here is a look at 10 books, nine films and eight songs that, in one way or another, revolve around an eclipse.

10 books marked by an eclipse

1. 'The Odyssey' (Homer, 8th century BC) In Book 20 of the poem, the seer Theoclymenus interprets a sudden darkening of the sky as heralding the imminent death of Penelope's suitors, shortly before Odysseus confronts them.

A study published in 2008 linked that passage to a real eclipse observed in the Ionian Islands in 1178 BC. The work is currently on everyone's lips because of Christopher Nolan's film, although that episode is not mentioned in the movie.

2. The 'Song of Roland' (anonymous, 11th century) This medieval epic poem, which tells of the defeat of Roland and his army at Roncesvalles at the hands of the Saracens, describes a sudden darkening of the sky, storms and an earthquake as signs of a possible end of the world. It is a classic example of how medieval literature associated eclipses with ill omens.

3. 'A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court' (Mark Twain, 1889) Hank Morgan, a mechanic from Connecticut, travels back in time to 6th-century England and is sentenced to death by burning at the stake. He then remembers that a solar eclipse is approaching and threatens to plunge the world into darkness if his life is not spared, which allows him to escape and earn a reputation as a sorcerer at King Arthur's court.

A Yankee in King Arthur's Court Anaya

4. 'King Solomon's Mines' (H. Rider Haggard, 1885) A few years before Twain, Haggard had already resorted to a very similar device: an explorer who knows the date of an imminent eclipse persuades the Kukuana tribe that he can hide the Sun with his powers, and in exchange demands that the people obey his orders.

5. Diaries (Virginia Woolf) The author of 'Mrs Dalloway' travelled in 1927 to the north of England to witness the first total eclipse visible in the country in almost 200 years. In her diaries she describes how the light disappeared completely for a few seconds and then returned all at once, which she herself noted as the most astonishing moment of the experience.

Portrait of Virginia Woolf (25 January 1882 – 28 March 1941), British writer and feminist. Wikimedia Commons

6. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Stephen King, 1992) The protagonist plans her husband's death, a violent, alcoholic man, taking advantage of the real solar eclipse that could be seen in the United States in 1963. Years later, during a police interrogation over another death, she recalls that episode to the investigators.

7. 'Gerald's Game' (Stephen King, 1992) Published in the same year as 'Dolores Claiborne', this novel also assigns a key role to the 1963 eclipse, which King used as the backdrop for two different stories told in very different tones.

8. 'Nightfall' (Isaac Asimov, 1941) On the planet Lagash, permanently lit by six suns, its inhabitants have no concept of darkness. When astronomers announce that a total eclipse will leave the planet without light for the first time in 2,000 years, society is confronted with something for which it is utterly unprepared. It is regarded as one of the best science-fiction short stories of the last century.

Nightfall Isaac Asimov

9. 'The Eclipse' (Augusto Monterroso, 1959) In this very short Guatemalan story, a Spanish friar lost in the jungle tries to save himself from being sacrificed by a group of Maya by warning them that, thanks to his knowledge, he is capable of darkening the Sun. The ironic ending turns his expectations completely on their head.

10. 'Total Eclipse' (Annie Dillard, 1982) This essay, included in the book "Teaching a Stone to Talk", recounts the author's journey to the Yakima Valley in Washington State to observe a total eclipse in 1979. Dillard describes the experience as something that completely transforms one's perception of reality, far more unsettling than she herself had expected.

Eclipse inspiration on screen

1. 'Barabbas' (Richard Fleischer, 1961) To film the crucifixion scene in this epic production, the crew timed the shoot to coincide with a real solar eclipse that took place in Italy on 15 February 1961, and deployed more than 40 cameras across Tuscany to capture the phenomenon's strange light.

2. 'Eclipse' (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1962) That same Italian eclipse of 1961 inspired Antonioni to choose the title of this film, starring Alain Delon and Monica Vitti, one of the classics of European cinema of the 1970s.

3. 'Ladyhawke' (Richard Donner, 1985) The two protagonists of this medieval fantasy, played by Michelle Pfeiffer and Rutger Hauer, are under a curse that turns her into a hawk during the day and him into a wolf at night. Only a solar eclipse, a day without night and a night without day, allows them to recover their human form at the same time.

'Ladyhawke', released in Spain as 'Lady Halcón' and under various titles in Latin America, is a fantasy, romance and adventure film directed by Richard Donner. IMDb

4. 'Apocalypto' (Mel Gibson, 2006) Set on the Yucatán peninsula in the early 16th century, the film shows its protagonist about to be sacrificed atop a Maya pyramid when a solar eclipse, interpreted by the priests as a sign from the Sun god, allows him to save his life.

5. 'Dolores Claiborne' (Taylor Hackford, 1995) A film adaptation of Stephen King's 'Dolores Claiborne', starring Kathy Bates and Jennifer Jason Leigh, which retains the central role of the 1963 eclipse in the plot.

6. 'Gerald's Game' (Mike Flanagan, 2017) Netflix's version of Stephen King's novel of the same name, starring Carla Gugino, which also brings back the 1963 eclipse as a central narrative element.

Carla Gugino in 'Gerald's Game' (2017) IMDb

7. 'Darkness' (Jaume Balagueró, 2002) In this horror thriller, a family moves into a house near Barcelona where, 40 years earlier, six children had been sacrificed in a ritual that coincided with a solar eclipse.

8. 'Venus' (Jaume Balagueró, 2022) The director of 'Darkness' once again turned to the motif of the eclipse in this film, in which a demonic entity tries to possess the protagonist, played by Ester Expósito, during the phenomenon.

9. 'Verónica' (Paco Plaza, 2017) Set during the 1991 solar eclipse in Madrid, the protagonist holds a seance with a ouija board in the middle of the phenomenon, with consequences that shape the rest of the film.

Eclipse in music

1. 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', Bonnie Tyler (1983) Written and produced by Jim Steinman, it became the biggest hit of the Welsh singer's career and a classic that gets played every time there is an eclipse anywhere in the world. Tyler died last July at the age of 75, just a few weeks before this eclipse, which her song has ended up turning into the phenomenon's unofficial anthem. Link:

2. 'Eclipse', Pink Floyd (1973) The track closes the album 'The Dark Side of the Moon' with a melody that builds to a climax and ends with the same heartbeat that opens the record, thus completing the circle of the whole album. Link:

3. 'You're So Vain', Carly Simon (1972) In one of its most memorable verses, the singer tells how the song's protagonist flies by private jet to Nova Scotia, in Canada, to witness a total solar eclipse, one of pop's most frequently cited references to this phenomenon. Link:

4. 'Eclipse Total del Amor', Lissette (1984) A Spanish-language version of 'Total Eclipse of the Heart', recorded by Cuban singer Lissette for her album 'Caricatura', with its own lyrics that depart in part from the original and that became a hit in Spanish-speaking countries. Link:

5. 'Eclipse' (feat. Los Macorinos), Natalia Lafourcade (2018) Included on 'Musas, Vol. 2', the album in which the Mexican singer pays tribute to Latin American folk music together with guitar duo Los Macorinos, this song uses the image of a lunar eclipse to describe the sadness of heartbreak. Link:

6. 'Eclipse de Luna', Luciano Pereyra (2000) A track from the Argentine singer's album 'Recordándote' that uses the image of a lunar eclipse as a metaphor for a night of passion. Link:

7. 'Total Eclipse', Klaus Nomi (1981) The German singer and countertenor, one of the most singular figures of New York post-punk, turned the eclipse into a metaphor for a nuclear catastrophe in this song, one of the most memorable tracks of his career, which he first performed at the festival "Urgh! A Music War" in 1980. Link:

8. 'Bad Moon Rising', Creedence Clearwater Revival (1969) Written by John Fogerty, it does not speak of an eclipse in the strict sense, but its lyrics about earthquakes, storms and dire omens under a menacing moon have made it a regular feature of playlists devoted to astronomical phenomena and dark portents. Link:

Bonus track

'Eclipse', Delta Goodrem (2026) The Australian singer represented her country at Eurovision 2026 with this track, written together with Jonas Myrin, Ferras Alqaisi and Michael Fatkin, which uses the image of an eclipse as a metaphor for a love that aligns two different worlds in a perfect instant.

The video, shot on the dunes of Newcastle, stages that crossing between light and shadow. The song reached the final of the festival, held in Vienna, where it finished in fourth place. Link:

At Euronews we will be offering live coverage of the eclipse, so if you cannot get to the eclipse path in Spain, or if you are outside Spain, we invite you to join us to experience the total solar eclipse, a rare event that has not occurred in the Iberian Peninsula for more than 100 years.

World.title: Remarkable find: story behind Wehrmacht motorbike recovered from the Danube
World.content:
The water level in the Danube has never been this low. The low water is exposing what has lain hidden on the riverbed for decades, including a Wehrmacht motorcycle of the DKW NZ 350-1 type from the Second World War. DKW is the abbreviation of "Dampfkraftwagen", a former German car and motorcycle brand from the Saxon motor city of Zschopau that was later taken over by Auto Union.

 

Low water: Wehrmacht motorcycle found in the mud of the Danube in central Budapest. (c) Volksbund Volksbund

The motorcycle was found in the riverbed in the heart of Hungary's capital, Budapest, level with the Hungarian parliament building. For staff at the local Institute and Museum of Military History it is a genuine find of the century. According to the institute, the vehicle is almost completely intact. It was effectively preserved in the Danube's mud.

DKW racing motorcycles from 1939 and 1931, archive Copyright 2007 AP. All rights reserved.

The motorcycle recovered is a model developed specifically for wartime use and built from 1944 onwards. It was powered by a two-stroke engine producing 11.5 hp. Thanks to their robustness and reliability, the bikes were popular with the troops. One of the distinctive features of the DKW 350-1 is the metal pannier on the side, a feature also present on the bike lifted from the Danube.

Around 12,000 units were produced by the end of the war in 1945. According to the ADAC, the predecessor model, the DKW (source in German) NZ 350, had a top speed of 105 km/h. Motorcycles were mostly used by the Wehrmacht as dispatch, reconnaissance or courier bikes.

German troops driving through Liège in Belgium, 30 May 1940 AP

The motorcycle was built by Auto Union AG, a car and motorcycle manufacturer founded in 1932 which at the time was the second-largest producer after Opel. Auto Union AG was created through the merger of several brands, including Audi.

On earlier models by the manufacturer, the frame components were still bolted together; on the NZ series they were welded. Because this required a high power supply, the welding could only be carried out at night, when the grid was not under strain from other users.

German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines, remnants of hand grenades and artillery shells were also found on the bed of the Danube. According to the Hungarian Institute of Military History, this stretch of the Danube may have been used as a "war rubble dump".

The motorcycle was discovered on 2 August on the Buda side of the Hungarian parliament, next to the harbour at Batthyány Square. Volksbund Volksbund

From March 1944, German troops laid siege to Budapest. Between October 1944 and February 1945, the Battle of Budapest was fought between the Soviet Red Army and German and Hungarian forces. Around 30,000 German, more than 17,000 Hungarian and some 80,000 Soviet and Romanian soldiers were killed. On 13 February 1945, the remaining German units surrendered.

After the war, the DKW production facilities were dismantled and taken to the Soviet Union as part of war reparations. In Moscow and other locations, they were used until 1951 to produce, in large numbers, the largely identical ISCH-350.

Human remains were found beneath the motorcycle. The Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge (German War Graves Commission) handled the recovery and says they are the mortal remains of two Wehrmacht soldiers. The crew of the motorcycle? Their identity tags are well preserved, so they should be able to be identified. The two dead soldiers are to be buried at the German war cemetery in Budaörs, west of Budapest. More than 16,000 German soldiers are already buried there.

The Volksbund is a non-profit association which, on behalf of the federal government, searches for, recovers and buries war dead abroad. In 2025 alone, it recovered and buried more than 5,500.

World.title: Russia bars its only anti-war party from September elections
World.content:
Russia's Supreme Court on Monday annulled the opposition Yabloko party's registration for the country's parliamentary elections, scheduled for September.

 

The ruling, which sidelines the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow's war ‌in Ukraine, came after the pro-Kremlin nationalist Rodina party filed a lawsuit last Friday, seeking to remove Yabloko from the elections.

Reacting to the Supreme Court decision, Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov said that "there are no grounds at all for removing the party from the elections."

"All the documents had been checked by the Central Election Commission, and the decision to allow us to run was taken unanimously," Rybakov said, recalling that Russia's Justice Ministry had repeatedly probed the party for various violations but found nothing illegal.

He described Rodina's claims as unsubstantiated and groundless.

Rodina leader and State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov argued that "lawyers have found numerous violations" in Yabloko's election campaign.

According to him, "first and foremost this is foreign funding that does not go through the account", as well as "extensive activity on banned social networks, which is financed from the West".

Zhuravlyov and Rodina accused Yabloko of "extremism," saying they saw "signs" of it in the party's call for peace.

Rodina also accused Yabloko of receiving funding from abroad and supporting the so-called "international LGBT movement," which is illegal under Russian law.

Leaders of other Russian parties also levelled accusations against Yabloko.

Chair of the Central Committee of the far-left Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF) Gennady Zyuganov blamed his opponents for not supporting "the policy of strengthening Russian statehood" and for "never once condemning the actions" of the Ukrainian authorities.

Ultranationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) leader Leonid Slutsky called for Yabloko to be designated an undesirable organisation because of its proposal to enter into peace talks with Kyiv.

Sergei Mironov, leader of left-wing nationalist A Just Russia party, said that the Justice Ministry and the Prosecutor General's Office should "take a close look at Yabloko because the party 'opposes the (war in Ukraine)', 'promises to conclude a peace that would disgrace the country' and 'supports foreign agents'".

Russia's Central Election Commission registered Yabloko's list for the parliamentary elections on 29 July.

The only anti-war party in Russia or a spoiler?

Running under the slogan "For peace and freedom," Yabloko is a social-liberal party platforming on anti-nationalism and demanding urgent political reforms in Russia.

Its election programme, made up of just 43 words, calls for "a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy, and the achievement of peace."

For many, the registration of a party advocating an end to the war came as a surprise and has prompted much speculation about how and why this could have happened, including claims that the initial approval was itself a Kremlin-orchestrated manoeuvre.

"A source close to the Central Election Commission believes that the logic behind allowing it is likely this: the authorities need a channel through which citizens can 'vent' their discontent," investigative outlet Important Stories wrote.

"Better into Yabloko than into spoiling ballot papers or voting for the Communist Party."

"Yabloko was registered according to a plan by the presidential administration. After the elections, the party's low official result can be presented as the share of Russians who oppose the war," Radio Liberty quotes political analyst Ivan Preobrazhensky as saying.

Another widely circulated claim or belief is that the Russian authorities need Yabloko to divert votes from the increasingly popular New People party.

"Yabloko has been let into the elections to take down 'New People'," writes Alexander Kynev, a specialist in Russia's regional political processes, on social media.

The nominally centrist New People party has also been accused of being a Kremlin-sanctioned outlet for protest votes.

Elections to the State Duma, along with voting for other levels of government, will take place in Russia on three days, from 18 to 20 September.

World.title: Kazakhstan offers crypto amnesty as it seeks to bring billions in digital assets home
World.content:
When Kazakhstan became one of the world's largest crypto mining hubs five years ago, the boom strained the country’s power grid, and the government’s response resulted in most miners either leaving the country or going underground.

 

Now the Kazakh government is looking to bring it all back home by offering tax breaks and legal certainty.

The Kazakh government signed a decree designed to encourage citizens to declare cryptocurrency holdings, move them onto regulated domestic platforms and integrate digital assets into the country's economy.

The authorities are offering private investors a tax break on personal income from digital asset transactions for three years, provided the assets were not connected to fraud, money laundering or linked to unlicensed crypto services.

The decision has opened the door to making it easier for miners to operate in the country — and for everyone to profit.

Crypto boom cut short

Cryptocurrency mining uses powerful computers to solve complex mathematical problems in order to verify and add transactions to a blockchain — the ledger on which a cryptocurrency's transaction history is recorded.

Miners who successfully complete them are rewarded with cryptocurrency deposited directly to their personal crypto wallets, which in some cases like Bitcoin can bring in significant profits.

The downside is that the process consumes a large amount of power because the computations require sustained processing.

After China banned Bitcoin mining in 2021, many miners began looking for new locations with low-cost energy.

At that point Kazakhstan rapidly became the second-largest Bitcoin mining location after the US. Many tried to get in on the profits, with people even putting mining equipment on their balconies.

Some went so far as to masquerade the mining farms as vegetable storage facilities, greenhouses or AI data centres at abandoned Soviet-era industrial sites to conceal their massive electricity consumption.

Aeral view of Alem Crypto Mining, a legal mining company in the north of Kazakhstan. Copyright: Alem Crypto Mining company

The country did not get to enjoy the crypto bloom for too long. The rapid influx of miners placed an enormous burden on the country’s ageing electricity grid.

In October 2021, surging electricity demand contributed to outages at three power plants in northeastern Kazakhstan, while rolling blackouts affected several regions. At peak, cryptocurrency miners were consuming an estimated 8% of Kazakhstan's total electricity output.

Authorities responded by repeatedly tightening regulations on electricity consumption and digital asset legalisation, leading to miners' departure abroad and the proliferation of illegal operations.

Kazakhstan never outright banned crypto mining, keeping its options open to potentially harness its potential in the future.

According to Kazakhstan's financial regulator, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakh citizens own approximately 1 million crypto wallets.

The AIFC, modelled on Dubai's DIFC financial free zone, has functioned as Kazakhstan's sandbox for financial innovation and serves as the regulatory home for digital asset companies operating in the country.

This figure is nearly four times the number of users registered on authorised local exchanges, which in March reached 256,900.

Bringing crypto assets back onshore

Attracting crypto owners back to their home countries with incentives and simplified legal frameworks has turned into a global trend in recent years, experts say.

The UAE, Hong Kong and Singapore have implemented similar tax measures alongside clear licensing, regulations and access to banking services, bringing in additional revenue.

The decree also addresses the energy question that triggered Kazakhstan's earlier mining crisis.

Under the plan, associated gas from oil fields not required for state use can be used to generate electricity for mining operations, broadening miners' options beyond the main national grid.

General Manager of Binance Kazakhstan Nurkhat Kushimov believes the tax incentive is the most important measure in the decree.

“This is a strong incentive for users to choose regulated jurisdictions and platforms operating within them," Kushimov told Euronews.

"This approach makes working in a licensed environment more attractive, fosters trust in the market and creates the conditions for its further development,” he said.

Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Association of Fintech, AI and Crypto Industry Bakhytzhan Kenzhebayev believes that the tax incentive removes one of the main uncertainties for the private investor, namely the question of when and on what basis the obligation arises. But the measure in itself is not sufficient.

“Users choose a platform not based on the tax rate, but on a combination of factors: how easy it is to deposit and withdraw (the local currency), the liquidity, and how clear the rules are,” Kenzhebayev told Euronews.

"For a licensed participant, the predictability of the rule is more valuable than the benefit itself."

President of Kazakhstan’s Blockchain and Digital Mining Association Daniyar Mubarakov told Euronews that any government support is welcome, but wonders how long this measure will work.

“For certain categories of entrepreneurs preferential tax regimes mean not only a reduction in taxes in the current period, but also a possible several-fold increase in taxes in the future due to increased volumes,” Mubarakov said.

Vice Minister of AI and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said that his department is working on a proposal for a simplified tax regime following the expiration of the exemption in three years' time.

He added that the department is also working on cancelling tax audits for private investors covering the previous three years.

Beyond tax incentives

Experts say that Kazakh private investors' return to domestic platforms will depend on their competitiveness.

“For most users, convenience of service, liquidity, availability of instruments, speed of transactions, and the ability to seamlessly interact with the banking system remain the key factors,” Kushimov said.

According to Kenzhebayev, the main risks now lie in the legal definitions and terminology used. If the exemption is defined too broadly, it could create space to abuse the system and avoid paying taxes on other assets unrelated to crypto.

“This creates the risk of a reversal of the norm in a year or two, and that causes more damage to the market than an initially high but stable rate,” Kenzhebayev explained.

He also warned that the same digital asset can be treated as two different things depending on whether it falls under the AIFC or Kazakhstan's national rules, which would in turn mean companies would have to comply with two separate legal structures at once.

"The difficulty arises at the intersection. As a result, the participant builds two parallel infrastructures for one business, which reflects on the costs," he said.

Kenzhebayev said tax breaks alone would not be enough to draw users to licensed Kazakh platforms.

What would make the difference, he said, is reliable access to banking, clear rules for converting crypto into the local currency, straightforward requirements for keeping client assets safe, and a regulatory environment that does not put licensed operators at a disadvantage.

World.title: Dog-friendly beaches in Spain 2026: Where to swim with your pet this summer
World.content:
More and more people are choosing to travel with their dog on holiday. However, not all Spanish beaches allow pets, especially in high season. To avoid fines or other problems, it is advisable to check in advance which beaches are dog-friendly and to find out about the specific rules in each municipality.

 

Spain currently has more than 100 dog beaches spread along its coastline, according to the specialist website Patitas&Co.

The Valencian Community, Catalonia, Andalusia and Murcia have the highest concentration of these areas, although there are also options in Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands.

The regions with the most options

The Valencian Community is one of the regions with the highest number of dog-friendly beaches. Some of the best known include Agua Amarga, in Alicante; Caleta dels Gossets, in Santa Pola; Punta del Riu, in El Campello; and Pinedo beach, in Valencia. Catalonia also offers plenty of alternatives, such as La Rubina, in Castelló d'Empúries; Rec del Molí, in L'Escala; or Els Griells, in L'Estartit.

In Andalusia, designated beaches in the provinces of Málaga, Almería and Cádiz stand out, while Murcia has several specific areas for pets. Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands also offer spaces where dogs are allowed in the water all year round or at certain times of the year.

Always check the local regulations

Although the number of options grows every summer, most Spanish beaches still ban dogs during the summer season. Restrictions are set by each local council, so it is essential to check the rules before you travel.

Some beaches require animals to be kept under control at all times, while others insist on having up-to-date health documentation or restrict access to certain times of day.

Advice for going to the beach with your dog

If you are planning a day at the beach with your pet, vets recommend avoiding the hottest hours, taking enough water to keep your dog hydrated and making sure there are shaded areas available.

It is also important to always pick up your dog's waste, respect other beachgoers and keep an eye on their paw pads, as the sand can reach very high temperatures in summer.

World.title: Why a soccer field in one German city may become a flood zone
World.content:
Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from wildfires to storms are here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel in Germany are trying.

In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast. It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.

Human-made climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink how it works and is designed. It has since become a frontrunner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.

Is climate adaptation giving up on fighting climate change?

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage.

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the US to Quezon City in the Philippines , as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

Quezon City has also intensified its adaptation plans as days are getting hotter Image: Aaron Favila/AP Photo/picture alliance

That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," added Baum.

Redesigning cities for unavoidable impacts

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information, and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.

Kolkata's tree ambulance rushes to save urban trees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.

"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.

The research requires patience.

"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.

Living differently: No more daytime soccer?

Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

It might become the new normal to play only during certain times of the day Image: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.

How to reach people who don't think about the climate?

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.

At Kiel Week, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

The 2023 storm surge caused caused millions of euro in damage in the port city of Kiel Image: Daniel Bockwoldt/dpa/picture alliance

"People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.

Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.

Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.

"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.

Climate adaptation not 'optional'

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 US court dismisses bribery and fraud charges against billionaire Adani

In May, the US government will settle a lawsuit filed against Gautam Adani, one of the world's richest people, for hiding an alleged bribery scheme. Image: Aijaz Rahi/AP Photo/picture alliance

A US judge on Monday dismissed bribery and fraud charges against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after the Trump administration moved to drop the case.

Adani, a close ally of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, was charged in 2024 of participating in a $265 million (€229.7 million) scheme to bribe Indian officials to secure solar energy contracts.

His associates were also charged with attempting to obstruct the US investigations by destroying evidence. Adani has denied wrongdoing.

Brooklyn federal judge Nicholas Garaufis criticized the US Justice Department's handling of the decision said the decision to dismiss the 2024 charges was unusual and raised concerns because prosecutors and investigators, including FBI and SEC agents involved in the case, were not consulted.

According to media reports Adani's attorney Robert Giuffra, who is also Donald Trump's personal lawyer, told Justice Department officials in April that if charges were dropped, the billionaire would invest $10 billion in the United States.

Garaufis said he believed that Adani's reported pledge to invest in the US did not influence the Justice Department's decision to drop the case.

In May, court documents showed that Gautam Adani agreed to pay civil penalties of $6 million, while his nephew Sagar Adani, another leader at Adani Green Energy, agreed to pay $12 million in a settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The proposed settlement doesn't include an admission of guilt.

Adani welcomed the ruling, saying his faith in "truth, fairness and the rule of law" remained unwavering.

World.title: Germany news: Rhine levels could cause production cuts
World.content:
08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 Child road accidents rising steadily

Children on bicycles are at particular risk of being killed or injured Image: Ralf Hirschberger/dpa/picture alliance

More children were killed or injured in road accidents in 2025 than in in the previous year. That represents a renewed rise in road deaths and injuries affecting children since a decline during the coronavirus pandemic, statistics show.

Altogether 29,270 children under the age of 15 were injured in traffic accidents in Germany last year, a 7% increase over 2024, the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Monday.

The number of children killed in such accidents also rose from 53 in 2024 to 74 in 2025.

Of those fatalities, 30 were children under 6, well up on the number of children in that age group that were killed in 2024 (18).

The largest increase in deaths was seen in children travelling in cars (21 to 31).

The number of children killed on their bicycles in 2025 rose to 13 from 8 the previous year, while 4 were killed riding e-scooters, compared with none in 2024.

Most of the children involved in road traffic accidents in 2025 were riding a bicycle (34%). Altogether 31% were in a car, 20% were on foot and 8% were travelling on an e-scooter when the accidents occurred

"On average, a child was injured or killed in a road traffic accident every 18 minutes in 2025," Destatis said.

World.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
World.content:
In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

A healthcare worker prepares an MMR vaccination at a health center in Texas [FILE: April 8, 2025] Image: Annie Rice/AP Photo/picture alliance

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long questioned established vaccine recommendations and promoted a disproven link between vaccines and autism Image: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA/picture alliance

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, has sharply criticized Trump's executive order on childhood vaccines, saying it could leave children less protected [FILE: May 19, 2026] Image: Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

World.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
World.content:
Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

What does Turkey's new PKK law provide?

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Turkish lawmakers debated the bill for around 12 hours before voting on the legislation Image: Mustafa Kaya/Xinhua/picture alliance

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

When will the law take effect?

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz hailed the vote as a 'historic step' toward ending the decades-long conflict with the PKK [FILE: March 27, 2026] Image: Ahmet Okur/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

What happens to Abdullah Ocalan?

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

This latest image of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was provided by the pro-Kurdish DEM party [FILE: February 27, 2026] Image: DEM

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

What does the PKK say?

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Why is the bill controversial?

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

Why does the conflict matter?

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus.

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Russia: Top court bans opposition anti-war party from vote
World.content:
Yabloko, Russia's only anti-war party, has been barred from September's parliamentary elections. The motion to bar Yabloko was filed by the nationalist pro-Kremlin party Rodina.

The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections.

Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things.

Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence.

The nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina party brought the case, accusing Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, yet without providing evidence to support the claim Image: Pavel Seleznev/TASS/picture alliance

On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted."

The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition.

Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities."

"We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision.

Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin.

The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003.

Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September.

Yabloko supporters ignored the threat of repression to show support for the party's anti-war stance at the Supreme Court Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia.

The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

The government has declared a state of emergency.

What is the latest?

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

More than 100 dead in Colombia after major earthquake To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.

"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

What's happening on the ground?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.

Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

World.title: Colombia, bajo el estado de emergencia por el terremoto que causa más de 130 muertos
World.content:
Colombia todavía cuenta sus muertos. El país amanecerá este martes bajo el estado de emergencia nacional, después de que un terremoto de magnitud 7,4 sacudió la víspera durante cuatro eternos minutos el oeste del país, y se sintió hasta Panamá y Ecuador. Los coletazos del temblor –el de mayor magnitud desde 1979– han dejado hasta el momento más de un centenar de muertos y más de 500 heridos, con decenas de edificios completamente colapsados. Al menos 132 personas han fallecido, de acuerdo con el más reciente balance de la Asociación Colombiana de Ciudades Capitales (Asocapitales). Las cifras todavía se consideran preliminares.

Una gran parte de las muertes se concentra en la ciudad de Pereira, en el eje cafetero. También ha quedado muy golpeada Cali, la capital del Valle del Cauca y la tercera ciudad más poblada del país, donde se declaró un toque de queda y se han militarizado varios puntos, especialmente las zonas donde aún se desarrollan acciones de rescate entre los escombros. Quibdó, la capital del Chocó, donde se ubicó el epicentro en San José del Palmar, así como Manizales y Armenia, vecinas de Pereira en la región cafetera, son otras de las urbes más afectadas, con edificios colapsados, aeropuertos cerrados y servicios intermitentes.

En Cali, que se preparaba para celebrar el popular festival de música del Pacífico Petronio Álvarez este fin de semana, los rescatistas todavía escarban entre los escombros en busca de sobrevivientes. Mientras que en la región cafetera el temblor ha revivido el trauma de otro terremoto, el que devastó Armenia en enero de 1999 y dejó a su paso casi 1.200 muertos.

Vista aérea de edificios colapsados por el temblor de este lunes, en Cali, Colombia ALEJANDRO MELÉNDEZ (EL PAÍS)

El desastre se ha desencadenado cuando el presidente, Abelardo de la Espriella, cumplía apenas tres días en el cargo, después de que se posesionó el viernes en un auditorio de Cali y pronunció su primer discurso desde una instalación militar, en el que prometió gobernar desde las regiones y para las regiones. “Le encomiendo nuestro país al señor Jesucristo”, dijo después del mediodía, cuando transmitió el primer reporte del Gobierno y declaró la emergencia nacional desde Bogotá, a donde voló por primera vez como mandatario desde la caribeña Barranquilla, la ciudad que propone convertir en capital alterna de un país con una geografía muy compleja.

En su primer lunes en el poder, cuando apenas ajusta su talante como gobernante, el presidente aseguró que “los compatriotas afectados” saldrán adelante “con la ayuda de Dios”, del Gobierno y de la cooperación internacional, e hizo un llamado a la unidad nacional: “Hoy todos los colombianos, sin distinciones ideológicas, tenemos que unirnos frente a una sola causa: las víctimas de este desastre natural”. Aseguró que asumía “directamente el liderazgo” de la atención de la emergencia. Un enorme primer desafío, en un momento prematuro para un Ejecutivo que apenas da sus primeros pasos.

En la tarde, realizó una fugaz visita al Chocó junto a parte de su gabinete, y de allí partió al Valle del Cauca. El presidente instaló un Puesto de Mando Unificado (PMU) nacional en Bogotá, y otros en Quibdó, Cali y Armenia. También decidió desplegar equipos liderados por varios de los ministros recién nombrados en algunos de los lugares más afectados.

Habitantes y autoridades buscan entre los escombros este lunes en Quibdó. Jean Arriaga (EFE)

Tanto el vicepresidente, José Manuel Restrepo, como el ministro del Interior, Rodrigo Lara, se encuentran en el eje cafetero, mientras que el de Defensa, el general retirado Jorge Eduardo Mora, y la de Salud, Ana María Vesga, están en Cali. Más allá del gabinete, y de su círculo más cercano, De la Espriella todavía no ha reemplazado las cabezas de algunas entidades clave para la atención de desastres, aunque ha anunciado que este martes designará al ingeniero geólogo David Suárez Tamayo en la cabeza de la Unidad Nacional de Gestión del Riesgo. Esa coyuntura se agravó por la ruptura del tradicional empalme con el anterior gobierno, en cabeza del izquierdista Gustavo Petro.

La solidaridad internacional se ha dejado sentir, a menos de dos meses de los terremotos de junio que devastaron a la vecina Venezuela con un saldo de más de 6.000 muertos. Estados Unidos anunció una ayuda de 15,5 millones de dólares, destinada a refugio de emergencia, alimentos, protección y evaluaciones de los daños causados por el sismo. También el Banco de Desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe (CAF) dará una donación de 500.000 dólares a Colombia para atender la emergencia. Hace apenas unas semanas, CAF había anunciado un paquete financiero de 9.000 millones de dólares para impulsar el desarrollo del país en el periodo 2026-2030, que coincide con el cuatrienio de De la Espriella.

Otros socios cercanos ideológicamente al nuevo Gobierno colombiano expresaron su apoyo y disposición a ayudar, como el argentino Javier Milei, el chileno José Antonio Kast o el ecuatoriano Daniel Noboa. Los tres asistieron el viernes pasado a la posesión de De la Espriella en Cali. También ofrecieron ayuda desde la otra orilla ideológica mandatarios como el brasileño Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, la mexicana Claudia Sheinbaum o el español Pedro Sánchez. La Organización de Naciones Unidas (ONU), con una larga historia de presencia en el país, se manifestó preparada para ayudar en lo que haga falta.

World.title: Dos senderos idóneos para explorar el Valle de Arán en verano
World.content:
En la zona occidental de la comarca pirenaica esperan la Artiga de Lin y la Val de Toran. Cascadas, mariposas, pequeños pueblos y antiguos caminos para el contrabando que se disfrutan sin multitudes

Que levanten la mano quienes hayan estado en Baqueira, Salardú o Artíes. ¡Hala, cuánta gente! Ese es el Naut Aran (el Alto Arán, en aranés), al que más de un millón de personas acuden en invierno a esquiar. Que la levanten ahora quienes hayan estado en Es Bòrdes o en Canejan. Ni la décima parte. Esta zona occidental del Valle de Arán, por la que corren el río Garona y la carretera N230 poco antes de entrar en Francia, no es tan famosa como la oriental, pero por eso mismo está rodeada de montañas silenciosas, virginales, sin remontes ni aparcamientos para 1.600 vehículos.

Cuando la nieve se retira, aquí se ven flores, mariposas y cascadas. Hay dos senderos idóneos para explorarla: el que recorre el pasmoso valle de la Artiga de Lin, donde surgen a chorros las aguas del glaciar del Aneto después de circular casi cuatro kilómetros bajo tierra, y el camino del Contrabando, entre Canejan y Sant Joan de Toran, por el que los vecinos traficaban durante la posguerra con café y azúcar de la vecina Francia.

Los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío

La Artiga de Lin es el paraje natural más espectacular de la comarca. En este valle glaciar hay dos lugares difíciles de creer: a 1.370 metros de altura, se encuentra la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu (­los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío, que de las tres formas lo traducen), donde brotan 1.580 litros de agua por segundo —y hasta 10.000 en pleno deshielo—. Cien metros más arriba, a 1.470, está el Plan dera Artiga, una gran pradera alpina rodeada de hayedos, abetales y escarpadas montañas calizas a casi 3.000 metros de altura donde lindan el Valle de Arán y el de Benasque, Lleida y Huesca, Cataluña y Aragón.

Surgencia de los Uhels deth Joèu, en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

A diferencia de lo que ocurre en la zona oriental del Valle de Arán, aquí no se puede aparcar a pie de pista porque no hay ninguna. Tampoco hay atascos porque los meses de mayor afluencia de visitantes en esta zona, los estivales, es obligatorio estacionar junto a la ermita dera Mair de Diu dera Artiga de Lin, tres kilómetros antes de llegar al final de la estrecha carretera que sube culebreando por el valle desde el pueblo de Es Bòrdes. Luego se puede continuar subiendo por el asfalto en un trenecito turístico o hacerlo a pie por el camino del Agua, que es una senda ribereña fácil y preciosa.

Siguiendo el camino, antes de una hora se verá la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu. “¿De dónde sale tanta agua?“, se preguntan todos los que examinan por primera vez este nacedero torrencial, porque aunque su caudal medio se reduce en verano a 250 litros por segundo, sigue siendo mucha fuente. Pues resulta que sale del Aneto, el techo de los Pirineos, en la vecina Huesca. Y se sabe porque, en 1931, el espeleólogo francés Norbert Casteret vertió 60 kilos de colorante inocuo en el Forau d’Aigualluts —un sumidero kárstico del valle de Benasque donde las aguas recién fundidas del glaciar del Aneto desaparecen bajo tierra después de pegar un buen salto—, y comprobó que estas aparecían teñidas en los Uelhs. Así que estas aguas nacidas al sur de los Pirineos, en vez de ir al Ebro y al Mediterráneo, que sería lo lógico, corren cuatro kilómetros bajo las montañas para engrosar el río Garona y acabar en el Atlántico.

Indicador de rutas en la Artiga de Kin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Flores mil, más de 150 mariposas y dos guías excelentes

Al pie de la cascada tumultuosa, hay una pasarela metálica que permite cruzar el río Joèu para seguir subiendo por el abetal de la margen contraria y acabar saliendo, tras dos horas de paseo, al Plan dera Artiga de Lin. Es un rellano glaciar bellísimo, presidido por la mole rocosa del Malh dera Artiga (2.711 metros) y alfombrado de prados llenos de flores —gencianas, astrancias, violetas de los Pirineos, geranios silvestres, consueldas mayores, malvas moscadas…— y mariposas de montaña: la apolo, la mnemosine, la colias alpina, la erebia oeme, la común, la dentada…

Para distinguir las más de 150 especies que viven en este Shangri-La de las mariposas, es sumamente útil la guía ilustrada que ha publicado el Conselh Generau d’Aran. Otra guía excelente para explorar la Artiga de Lin es Sara Arjó, bióloga que dirige la empresa de ecoturismo y educación ambiental Verd e Blu y que es la autora de Parpalhòles dera Val d’Aran, un juego didáctico de papiroflexia con 14 recortables de mariposas de siete especies, las más llamativas del lugar.

Mariposa zygaena osterodensis en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

Todo es bonito en la Artiga de Lin, hasta el espléndido refugio donde Arjó se toma un refresco y algún tentempié con sus clientes, dejándolos disfrutar un rato largo de este paisaje embobador antes de acercarse al siguiente lugar destacado de la ruta: la cascada de Pomèro. En esta última, a solo 300 metros del refugio, les presenta la amapola amarilla (Papaver cambricum), una flor rara en España, pero muy abundante y estimada en las islas británicas, a tal punto que la usa como emblema Plaid Cymru, el partido nacionalista que ahora gobierna en Gales. Una microcentral eléctrica produce en este florido salto la energía de la que se abastece el refugio, que es grandecito, con habitaciones para 27 montañeros y un buen restaurante para cualquiera que pase.

Vista al Aneto desde el mirador de Vilamòs

Desde el refugio se baja cómodamente por la carretera asfaltada hasta la ermita donde se aparcó al principio. Como no se tarda mucho en completar la vuelta a pie (la ruta circular descrita, de algo menos de ocho kilómetros, lleva hacerla unas tres horas, cuatro con paradas contemplativas y de refresco), hay tiempo para acercarse en coche al mirador de Vilamòs, que está a solo siete kilómetros de la Artiga de Lin en línea recta, pero a 17 por una carretera loca (la LV5055) que sube desde El Pont d’Arròs trazando 16 revueltas. El mirador no está señalizado en la carretera, pero sí en Google Maps.

Vista del refugio de la Artiga de Lin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Desde aquí, con la ayuda del móvil y de la aplicación AR AlpineGuide (disponible en Google Play y en Apple Store), pueden identificarse las montañas que se alzan alrededor de la Artiga de Lin, arropando su formidable recuenco glaciar: la doble cima de la Forcanada, el Malh dera Artiga, la Tuca Blanca de Pomèro… Detrás de esta última cumbre asoman las nieves perpetuas y los riscos estratosféricos del macizo de la Maladeta, señoreados por el Aneto (3.404 metros).

Después de este atracón de montañas, apetece bajar a El Pont d’Arròs para darse otro de cocina aranesa en el restaurante del hotel Peña. Este es un cuatro estrellas cómodo y hogareño a más no poder, al que solo le falta aire acondicionado en las habitaciones para ser extraordinario. Pronto lo instalarán: el cambio climático obliga. Luego, un baño en la piscina climatizada y a la cama, que mañana hay que madrugar para explorar otra cara oculta de Arán, su rincón más desconocido y solitario: la Val de Toran.

Republicanos, judíos, maquis y contrabandistas

En Puntaut, poco antes de que el río Garona se cuele en Francia y de que la carretera N230 española se convierta en la N125 gala, se desvía a la derecha otra muy estrecha, sin eje central y sumamente virada que se adentra en la recóndita Val de Toran. Seis kilómetros y 38 curvas más arriba, se llega a Canejan, un pueblecito-balcón que domina desde su altura un inmenso panorama ­de las montañas donde España y Francia se besan.

Una cruz occitana en en suelo de la Plaça dera Castra, en Canejan. Andrés Campos

En la Plaça dera Castra, la mayor y más cuidada, la del Ayuntamiento, de pavimento decorado con una gran cruz occitana —la enseña aranesa—, dos paneles informativos recuerdan que por Canejan pasaban a Francia no pocos republicanos que huían de la represión franquista tras la Guerra Civil y judíos que escapaban en dirección contraria, de la Europa ocupada por los nazis, durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. También recuerdan que esta fue la primera localidad atacada y tomada por los guerrilleros antifranquistas en octubre de 1944 durante la llamada Operación Reconquista de España, que pretendía deponer al dictador y restaurar la República. No dicen nada, en cambio, de los contrabandistas que trajinaban aquí en los años del hambre y del racionamiento, entre 1939 y 1952. Para decirlo, están los vecinos. No es que haya muchos en la Val de Toran (unos cien), pero casi todos están en Canejan. Una de ellas, Generosa Marqués, cuenta al que quiera oírla el caso de sus padres, Pedro y Palmira, que una vez al mes iban a la comuna gala de Fos y volvían cargados de café y azúcar, productos que escaseaban en el mercado regulado español y por los que sacaban un buen pico. Hasta que una noche los sorprendieron y pasaron las 15 siguientes entre rejas.

Difícil saber qué caminos usaban los contrabandistas para cruzar la raya. Como dice Generosa, “el tiempo, el del reloj y el atmosférico, los ha borrado”. Sin embargo, se conservan bien algunos de los que seguían para trapichear en este valle fronterizo, como el histórico que une Canejan, Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran. Para andar por él solo hay que subir a lo más alto de Canejan y salir del pueblo siguiendo la calle Era Cau, que pronto se hace de tierra, asciende dejando a la derecha unas rústicas bordas y se vuelve prácticamente llana. Para más señas, hay indicadores de dirección y marcas de pintura blanca y roja a lo largo de todo el recorrido, pues coincide con el sendero GR-211. Y se puede consultar el mapa y descargar el track de la ruta en Wikiloc.

La soledad de Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran

Tras una hora de paseo por este camino alto y horizontal, contemplando cómo desde una terraza el callejón sin salida montañoso de la Val de Toran, se entra en Porcingles, una aldea fantasma con solo dos casas temporalmente habitadas, calles impracticables y un lavadero cuyas aguas llevan tanto tiempo sin reflejar a un humano, que las mariposas (los sátiros del bosque y los ocelados, por citar dos especies que aquí se ven), se posan sobre las manos del recién llegado, sin saber qué es. Las ruinas de Porcingles son un recuerdo escalofriante de cuando a la Val de Toran llegó para quedarse una muchedumbre de 500 personas poseída por la fiebre del oro o, más bien, del zinc y del plomo, que eran lo que se sacaba de las minas de Liat, en la cabecera del valle, durante el siglo XIX y a principios del XX. Había incluso un teleférico de 13 kilómetros que transportaba todo lo extraído valle abajo, hasta el lavadero de mineral de Puntaut.

El camino, bastante llano hasta Porcingles, gana luego altura, cruza el barranco de Gotèrs y la pierde para llegar, al cumplirse dos horas de marcha, a Sant Joan de Toran. Tampoco es un lugar donde viva una multitud: solo tres personas. Pero junto a los prados que alguien se ha tomado la molestia de segar, hay una iglesia con macetas floridas a cada lado de la puerta y una docena larga de casas y bordas tradicionales de piedra en perfecto estado, en cuyos tejados de afilado caballete no falta una sola losa de pizarra: señal de que aquí viene a pasar cortas temporadas gente harta del mundanal ruido, que sabe lo que es bueno y que puede permitírselo. En este pueblo de postal se encuentra uno de los pocos negocios turísticos de la Val de Toran, el restaurante Estupendet, buen sitio para tomarse una ensaladilla rusa de verdad y una cerveza artesanal Refu. Este pulcro pueblecito rodeado de prados y montañas es lo más encantador del Valle de Arán, con permiso de la Artiga de Lin.

Nine people have arrested after police seized 586kg of drugs in a raid in a coastal suburb of The Hague.

Armed police guarded the entrance to a block of flats in Zeezwaluwhof, in Duindorp, on Thursday, as officers spent several hours searching the building.

Six people were arrested at the time of the search and three others in the following days. All but one are in custody pending a first court appearance on Wednesday.

The public prosecution service did not release further details of the suspects or charges, citing the ongoing investigation.

World.title: Hackers access Dutch credit card data in latest cyberattack
World.content:
