World.title: At least 19 dead due to storms, monsoon – NDRRMC
World.content:
CLEARING. Rescuers gather in Antipolo City on August 9, to retrieve a delivery rider covered by a fallen tree and utility pole.

At least 7,000 farmers are affected, while 5,000 hectares of farmland, or 85% of the affected area, are unlikely to recover

MANILA, Philippines – At least 19 people died due to the combined effects of the southwest monsoon, Tropical Depression Luis and Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira), the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council reported Tuesday, August 11.

Twelve of the recorded deaths were in Benguet, due to landslides. Four people died in Rizal and three in Batangas. Fifteen people were injured and four were reported missing. So far, the government has provided P73.5 million in assistance.

Antipolo City reported one fatality, a delivery rider who died after a tree and a Meralco utility pole fell on him. The city government has promised to assist the family through the wake and burial.

Farmers reeling from continuous rain

Meanwhile, the agriculture sector is dealing with at least P197.15 million in production value losses, the Department of Agriculture (DA) reported Tuesday. Areas adversely affected include Ilocos Region, Cagayan, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, and Western Visayas. Rice farmers were hit the hardest.

The DA was preparing P106.5 million worth of agricultural inputs to help farmers as of Monday, August 10.

“We need our people on the ground to move quickly so affected farmers can get the assistance they need, especially insurance claims and credit support,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said Monday. “The faster we process these, the faster farmers can recover and get back to production.”

At least 7,000 farmers were affected, while 5,000 hectares of farmland, or 85% of the affected area, are unlikely to recover.

The Philippine Space Agency’s mapping on August 6 showed rice farms in La Union and Pangasinan flooded. Agoo, La Union, and Calasiao, Pangasinan also had several flood areas.

MAP. The Philippine Space Agency mapped the extent of flooding in Region 1, August 6. Parts of the region are flooded due to the combined effects of Tropical Storm Maymay and the habagat.

– Rappler.com

World.title: DPWH seeks P107.4 billion for flood control projects in 2027
World.content:
Acting Budget Secretary Kim de Leon says that this is meant to support ongoing flood control projects

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is seeking P107.4 billion for flood control projects for 2027, a year after the government scrapped funding for such projects amid a corruption scandal.

Acting Budget Secretary Kim de Leon explained in a press briefing on Tuesday, August 11, that the funds are meant to support ongoing flood control projects.

“Hindi naman po natin puwedeng pabayaan ‘yung mga naumpisahan nang flood control projects. Mas hindi po magiging maayos ang epekto kung mananatiling nakatiwangwang ‘yung mga naumpisahan nang flood control projects,” De Leon said.

(We cannot neglect the flood control projects that are already underway. Abandoning these ongoing flood control projects will only lead to far worse consequences.)

De Leon also pointed out that flood control projects require spending beyond their initial construction costs, as some facilities come with recurring operating expenses. He cited pumping stations, which need to be maintained and operated every year.

During the previous budget deliberations, the DPWH scrapped P252 billion worth of locally funded flood control projects from the 2026 National Expenditure Program (NEP), following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive.

The decision came after the government uncovered substandard and ghost flood control projects across the country. Some government officials — including senators, congressmen, and DPWH personnel — allegedly benefited from these projects.

Under the Marcos administration, the funding for flood control projects spiked.

To prevent the recurrence of ghost projects, De Leon said the DPWH has ensured that projects included in the NEP are properly tagged, with identified locations and corresponding programs of work.

The DPWH got the second biggest allocation of P644 billion under the proposed 2027 budget. The allocation for the flood control project accounts for 16% of the agency’s total proposed allocation.

Aside from the DPWH allocation, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority is seeking P3.41 billion for its flood control program, including the operation of flood control structures. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler’s 2026 Board of Directors
World.content:
Former Microsoft CEO in the Philippines Peter Maquera is the new member of the Board

MANILA, Philippines – Former CEO of Microsoft Philippines Peter Maquera and veteran capital markets practitioner Gus Cosio are the latest members of the Board of Directors of Rappler, Inc.

Maquera joined the Rappler Board in July 2026, while Cosio became Board director in 2022. They joined the six existing members of the Rappler Board: Maria Ressa, Glenda Gloria, Manny Ayala, Winnie Monsod, Tony La Viña, and Federico Prieto.

In their meeting on July 3, 2026, the Board reelected Ressa as Board president and Gloria as chairperson.

Here are their brief profiles:

Manny Ayala, Director

Manny is a founder at Hatchd Inc, a technology incubator focused on building great Internet and mobile brands, and currently the global managing director of Endeavor Philippines. He was previously a managing director at IRG Ltd, a HK-based M&A boutique focused on the telecoms, media and tech industries. At IRG, Manny focused on a variety of projects in the Internet, mobile, television and online gaming sectors.

Manny was the number two executive at Discovery Networks Asia, instrumental in building Discovery Channel and Animal Planet into top-rated TV channels across the region. Prior to this, he served as deputy general manager for TNT and Cartoon Network Asia, an AOL Time Warner TV channel, where he was a key member of the team that launched the service across the Asia Pacific. Prior to that, Manny worked for STAR TV where he was part of the team that acquired the Don Bluth Animation Studio as well as a number of the world’s key Chinese-language film libraries. Manny has an MBA from the Harvard Graduate School of Business and a BA, cum laude, from Yale University.

Augusto “Gus” M. Cosio, Jr., Director

Gus retired as president of First Metro Asset Management Inc., a Metrobank subsidiary in June 2018 after joining the First Metro Investment Corporation Investment group in 2006 where he had been an active member of its investment committee.

His experience in investments and the capital markets span both local and international institutions. Gus had been an international capital markets practitioner for many years having been worked with Banque Nationale de Paris and Banque Paribas the predecessors of the present BNP Paribas prior to their merger. He worked in Hong Kong and Singapore for the Paribas capital markets group and in the Manila Off-shore Branch of Banque Nationale de Paris. He had been president of PNB Securities Inc. and a member of the board of the Philippine Stock Exchange. He also served as Senior Vice President of Security Bank Corporation and SB Capital Inc. Gus remains active in post retirement activities holding management positions and directorships in a few enterprises.

Glenda Gloria, Chairperson

Glenda co-founded Rappler in July 2011 and is currently its executive editor.

She has worked for the Philippine Daily Inquirer, The Manila Times, the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism, and for international news agencies. She co-founded the Philippines’ top investigative magazine Newsbreak, which started as a newsweekly and later merged with Rappler. From 2008 to January 2011, she managed ANC, the ABS-CBN News Channel, as its chief operating officer.

Glenda has written books on the military, conflict, and politics, among them the award-winning Under the Crescent Moon: Rebellion in Mindanao (with Marites Dañguilan Vitug). A British Chevening scholar, she holds a master’s degree in political sociology from the London School of Economics and Political Science. In May 2018, Glenda finished her Nieman journalism fellowship at Harvard University.

Antonio “Tony” La Viña, Director

Dean Antonio Gabriel La Viña is Associate Director of Manila Observatory where he heads the Klima Center and a professor of law, philosophy, politics and governance in several universities. He is the managing partner of La Viña Zarate and Associates, a development and social change progressive law firm and a member of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague: He is founding president of the Movement Against Disinformation Tony also writes for Rappler’s Thought Leaders section.

Peter Maquera, Director

Peter is former CEO of Microsoft Philippines, where he led the company’s efforts in cloud, AI, and cybersecurity. Earlier, Peter spent a significant portion of his career with the Ayala Group, notably as senior vice president of Globe Telecom’s Enterprise Group, president of Globe Telecom International Business Holdings, and deputy CEO of LiveIt Investments, Ltd., Ayala Corporation’s holding company for the BPO sector. Across his career his work centered on scaling complex ICT operations within the Philippines and across international markets.

Peter is a trustee of the Makati Business Club chairing the Philippine-US Business Council, and a trustee of the American Chamber of Commerce, co-chairing the ICT committee. Peter is also a member of the Private Sector Advisory Council (Digital Pillar), and a Board Advisor to the Asian Institute of Management RSN Center for Competitiveness. Peter earned his undergraduate degree in Engineering and a master’s in business administration from the University of Southern California.

Winnie Monsod, Director

An economist, teacher, writer and broadcaster, Winnie was appointed the Philippines’ first socio-economic planning secretary after the fall of the Marcos dictatorship in 1986. She is professor emerita at the University of the Philippines’ (UP) School of Economics, where she taught starting 1983.

Winnie served at the United Nations Committee on Development Policy and was convenor and member of the Advisory Board of the UNDP Human Development Report. For 11 years, she was chairperson of the Philippine Human Development Network. She also served on the advisory board of the South Centre in Geneva and the Board of Trustees of the International Food Policy Research Institute based in Washington, DC, and was a member of the High Level Task Force of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Winnie finished her degree in economics in UP and obtained her masters in economics at the University of Pennsylvania.

Federico “Fred” Prieto, Director

Fred is a lawyer with litigation and corporate practice. For his litigation practice he handles criminal, civil, labor and tax cases. His corporate practice involves mergers and acquisitions, business organization and restructuring, IPO offering and regulatory compliance, among others. He is a 2006 graduate of San Beda University’s College of Law in Mendiola and was admitted to the Bar in May 2007.

Maria Ressa, President

Maria is co-founder and CEO of Rappler. In October 2021, she was one of two journalists awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace.” In 2022, she was appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General to the Leadership Panel of the Internet Governance Forum and serves as its Vice-Chair. In March 2026, she was selected by the United Nations to sit on the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and serves as its Co-Chair.

She is a also a professor of practice at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. Maria authored Seeds of Terror: An Eyewitness Account of Al-Qaeda’s Newest Center of Operations in Southeast Asia and From Bin Laden to Facebook. Her most recent book, How to Stand Up to a Dictator, has been translated into more than 25 languages. – Rappler.com

World.title: This Puerto Princesa community rethinks plastic waste, builds a classroom out of it
World.content:
BAYANIHAN. Students, volunteers, and community members gather to prepare materials for Bahay Pangarap, working together through hands-on construction.

About 45 minutes from Puerto Princesa City proper, a small off-grid community in Barangay Bacungan is proving that sustainability begins with people

PALAWAN, Philippines – Beyond Puerto Princesa City’s bustling streets, a narrow road winds toward an off-grid community in Barangay Bacungan, where pristine beaches, forests, and a slower way of life surround Maia Earth Village, home to the Maia Earth Organization Incorporated founded in 2010.

About 15 minutes from the village stands Bahay Pangarap at Bacungan National High School (BNHS), a mud wall classroom built not only with earth from the community but also with more than 2,000 discarded plastic bottles transformed into ecobricks.

The project was made possible through the collaboration of Maia, Malaya Permakultura, and the Department of Education.

Bayanihan spirit

What began as an environmental initiative grew into a community-wide effort that brought together students, teachers, volunteers, and residents through the Filipino spirit of bayanihan.

Over two years, from 2023 to 2025, students collected plastic bottles, filled them tightly with nonbiodegradable waste to create ecobricks, and helped construct what Maia describes as the country’s first student-built mud wall classroom. It was completed in July 2025.

FEET AT WORK. Volunteers and students work together to mix the materials needed for the construction, making the building process a shared learning experience. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

For Pi Villaraza, founder of Maia Earth Organization Incorporated, Bacungan offered more than just a location for the project.

“Bacungan has a lot of potential to create these prototypes for sustainable communities,” Villaraza said. “It’s still accessible to the city, but it’s far away enough so that we can see the transition between the modern and the traditional lifestyles.”

He added that Bacungan is home to communities and initiatives striving to protect Palawan from development driven purely by profit, making it a fitting place to demonstrate sustainable living in practice.

Off-grid vision

Rather than using conventional construction methods, Bahay Pangarap was built using mud sourced from the village itself and ecobricks made from plastic bottles tightly packed with nonbiodegradable plastic waste.

Jesharelle Parcia, a Bacungan resident who helped build Bahay Pangarap, admitted she initially doubted the project would be completed because construction stretched over two years with long periods of inactivity.

“I didn’t think Bahay Pangarap would be finished because the progress wasn’t continuous,” Parcia said. “When it was finally completed, it felt fulfilling because we knew we were part of that dream. We stepped on the mud and filled the bottles until it all came together.”

For Graziele Burmann, a member of Maia Earth and a former teacher, the project’s greatest achievement was the enthusiasm it inspired among young people.

“It was really memorable to see their enthusiasm,” Burmann said. “Everyone got curious about ecobricks, the idea of painting with rocks. With time, everyone wanted to be part of it. The plan started small; we didn’t have to force anything, and things just happened naturally. It was just about strengthening the bond within the communities.”

BAHAY PANGARAP. It stands amid the greenery of Bacungan, Puerto Princesa, built through the collective efforts of students, volunteers, and the community using earth and ecobricks. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

Learning beyond the classroom

The construction site became an extension of the classroom itself.

“Normally, when you go to school, it’s theoretical,” Villaraza said. “But this project is active-based learning. We’re not just building the school; we’re also training the kids.”

Rhea Mae Tacan, a student at BNHS who helped build Bahay Pangarap, admitted she initially doubted that mud and plastic waste could be turned into a classroom.

“Seeing Bahay Pangarap finished made me realize how much waste we had transformed into something meaningful,” she said. “It showed that we can build without harming the environment.”

The initiative also encouraged residents to rethink plastic waste. Villaraza noted that improperly discarded plastic can persist for centuries, while burning it contributes to carbon emissions. Through ecobricks, he said, waste that would otherwise end up in landfills or the environment became a useful building material.

The impact extended beyond Bahay Pangarap. Villaraza recalled that students from BNHS organized a cleanup drive that reached the entire barangay, demonstrating how environmental stewardship can begin with young people and spread throughout the community.

CREATIVE LEARNING. Children take part in a creative activity at Maia Earth Village, where learning expands beyond conventional classrooms. Photo courtesy of Maia Earth Organization Inc.

Building a different future

For Burmann, however, the project’s lasting legacy is not measured by the classroom’s mud walls but by the mindset it helped cultivate.

“People need to see that it is possible,” she said. “If you don’t change the mindset, if you don’t show that there is a different way to see things, then it’s very hard to change.”

That mindset continues to shape Maia’s work beyond Bahay Pangarap.

The organization is currently building a health and wellness center with barangay partners and doctors to promote nutrition and natural medicine. It is also working with persons deprived of liberty, or PDLs, at Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm, introducing natural building as a therapeutic and rehabilitative activity.

Today, Bahay Pangarap stands as proof that when a community builds together, even discarded waste can become the foundation of dreams. – Rappler.com

Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The development communication editor of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

World.title: When courts, agencies stepped in to block wage hikes
World.content:
Other government bodies, apart from the NWPC and regional boards, blocked supposed wage hikes before

MANILA, Philippines – A month after the “historic” P85 minimum wage hike was promised for workers in Metro Manila, a Pasig City court temporarily halted the rollout.

It came after two construction companies raised concerns that the hike would disrupt projects that already went through bidding.

This is not the first time that a court, other government bodies, or officials intervened and blocked wage increases in the country.

According to the Wage Rationalization Act, the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC) and its regional counterparts can issue wage orders after public hearings, consultations, and deliberative meetings.

Congress may also introduce bills for wage hikes. The President and civil society groups can call on wage policy-making bodies to review and revise wages. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. made the same call in 2024.

The following are the interventions made by agencies and public officials in relation to regional and national wage hikes:

Pasig RTC suspends P85 NCR Wage Hike (2026)

The first tranche of P60 was implemented on July 25, 2026, with the additional P25 scheduled for next year, January 20, 2027.

However, Branch 152 of the Pasig Regional Trial Court issued a temporary restraining order against the regional wage board and the NWPC’s Wage Order No. 27 until August 13, following a petition by two construction companies.

Readycon Trading and Construction Corporation and R-II Builders argued that the sudden increase would affect existing projects that already went through bidding before the announcement. The two companies cautioned that the hike would reduce profits, make them less competitive in bidding, cut jobs, and even suspend operations.

The court found that the implementation may cause irreparable harm, as companies might have to adjust salaries to prevent wage compression.

However, the Federation of Free Workers and the Nagkaisa Labor Coalition pointed out that the order bypasses Article 126 of the Labor Code.

The code states that appeals must be filed with the NWPC or Regional Boards before any court can issue an injunction or temporary restraining order.

A hearing for a longer preliminary injunction was scheduled for August 3.

P100 hike dies after Congress sine die (2025)

A bill to increase the minimum wage by P100 died after the 19th Congress adjourned its annual session. It was the closest legislated increase since the 1989 hike before decentralization through the Wage Rationalization Act.

The 19th Congress had two versions of the hike. Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri filed Senate Bill No. 2534 proposing a P100 daily increase. The House of Representatives also had House Bill No. 11376, which called for a P200 increase in minimum wage.

Another bill must be introduced and passed in the 20th Congress to increase the daily minimum earnings of workers.

COVID-19 pandemic (2020)

During the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) secretary Silvestre Bello III discouraged having a minimum wage hike because of the economy’s fragility at the time.

Bello reasoned that job security was more important and that employers might not be able to meet the calls for a wage increase from P537 to around P700. DOLE believed that a hike during the pandemic would be counterproductive and would force micro, small, and medium businesses to close.

He cautioned that petitions made by labor groups to increase wages must be studied.

SC voids Cagayan wage order (2007)

The Supreme Court (SC) in 2007 voided Wage Order No. R02-03, which was issued in 1995.

The Court ruled that the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board of Region II overstepped its authority by granting an across-the-board wage increase for non-minimum wage earners.

This 1995 wage order implemented a P15 increase across-the-board in the region, regardless of employment status.

The Bankers’ Council for Personnel Management asked the NWPC whether member-banks with head offices in Metro Manila were exempt from the hike since their employees were already paid above the regional minimum wage.

Metrobank filed a petition directly with the Court of Appeals (CA). The CA denied the petition since the company failed to file within the proper period of 15 days after the decision.

Metrobank then elevated the petition to the SC. Years later, the High Court voided the wage increase, but ruled that workers should not be required to refund the amounts they had received and that the minimum wage would remain unchanged at the time.

SC voids rushed Cagayan wage order (1998)

Another wage order in Cagayan once again found itself in the middle of a legal battle. This time, the dispute centered on whether it had been rushed.

In 1994, DOLE discovered that Cagayan Sugar Milling Company (CARSUMCO) did not give the increase to its higher-earning employees and violated Wage Order No. RO2-02.

CARSUMCO filed an appeal, but DOLE ruled that the company had violated the wage order and ordered it to pay the salary deficiency worth P555,133.41.

The regional board later amended the wage order without holding the mandatory public hearings, resulting in the “across-the-board” wage increase in 1995 that Metrobank challenged years later.

After a back-and-forth between the company and DOLE, the SC issued a TRO pending resolution of the matter. In 1998, the SC ruled in favor of CARSUMCO, clearing the original penalty and declaring the wage order null and void. – Rappler.com

World.title: Celebrating John Gokongwei Jr., the man behind the developments
World.content:
Before he became one of the country’s most respected entrepreneurs, John Gokongwei Jr. was a young dreamer whose belief in possibility laid the foundation for generations of Filipinos

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Robinsons Land Corporation and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

As Robinsons Land celebrates the 100th birth anniversary of its founder, John Gokongwei Jr., it reflects on the values that defined his life and honors his legacy through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard, the newly renamed main thoroughfare of Bridgetowne.

Stretching approximately 1 kilometer and connecting Pasig City and Quezon City, the boulevard serves as the central spine of the estate. More than a road, it stands as a reminder of the vision, discipline, and long-term thinking that guided Mr. John throughout his life and continues to shape Robinsons Land today.

Long before Robinsons Land began building malls, homes, offices, hotels, and mixed-use developments across the Philippines, however, its founder was simply a young boy selling basic goods to help support his family.

When his father passed away, Mr. John, as he was fondly called, was only 13. As the eldest child, he suddenly found himself taking on greater responsibility. To earn money for the family, he and his mother cooked peanuts with garlic, packed them in small bags, and sold them, an experience he would later describe as his first as an entrepreneur.

YOUNG JOHN GOKONGWEI JR. A glimpse into the early life of the man who would go on to build some of the Philippines’ most enduring businesses.

By 15, he was waking before dawn and riding his bicycle several kilometers to the public market. There, he sold spools of thread, bars of soap, and candles, often working long after the other vendors had left. He used part of his earnings to buy food and reinvested the rest in more goods to sell.

From those early experiences grew a much larger vision, one grounded in understanding what people needed, creating opportunities, and building for the long term.

Today, visitors driving through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard will encounter a modern estate filled with offices, residences, retail destinations, and public spaces. Yet the journey behind the name began far from boardrooms and master-planned developments. It began with a young boy determined to help his family and create opportunities where few existed.

HONORING JOHN GOKONGWEI JR. JG Summit president and CEO Lance Y. Gokongwei and Robinsons Land president and CEO Mybelle V. Aragon-GoBio stand beside the newly inaugurated John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard in Bridgetowne.

A habit of learning

Hardship taught Mr. John to work hard, use his resources carefully, and keep moving forward. It also taught him to pay close attention to people: what they needed, what they could afford, and what would encourage them to return.

He remained deeply curious throughout his life. During long trading journeys by boat from Cebu to Manila, he spent the time reading books about people, places, and lives beyond his own experience. He later recalled that reading expanded his mind and helped him see possibilities he had not encountered before.

That curiosity became one of his greatest strengths. He studied markets, observed how consumers behaved, and looked for needs that existing businesses were not meeting.

Mr. John was careful with money and deliberate in his decisions, but he was not afraid to act. He reinvested what he earned, studied opportunities closely, and took calculated risks when he saw long-term potential. Rather than pursue quick gains, he focused on building businesses that could remain useful and relevant for generations.

Building around everyday needs

Mr. John’s experience of hardship also gave him an understanding of what access and opportunity could mean to Filipino families.

Across the businesses he founded, this belief took different forms. Affordable food products reached more households. Air travel became accessible to more Filipinos. Educational initiatives helped young people prepare for brighter futures, while growing enterprises created jobs and economic opportunities across the country.

Through Robinsons Land, this same philosophy took physical form.

UNVEILING A LEGACY. Robinsons Land’s key executives stand united beneath the John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard marker.

The company created places around the everyday lives of people: destinations where families could gather, businesses could flourish, travelers could stay, and communities could grow. Across malls, offices, residences, hotels, logistics facilities, and mixed-use developments, Robinsons Land sought to create environments that support how Filipinos live, work, and connect.

In many ways, Bridgetowne exemplifies this vision. Designed as an integrated community that brings together residential, commercial, office, hospitality, and public spaces, it reflects Mr. John’s belief in creating long-term value through thoughtful planning and connectivity. It is fitting that the estate’s main thoroughfare now bears his name.

A legacy that continues to guide

Since its establishment in 1980, Robinsons Land has grown into one of the country’s leading property developers, with developments spanning malls, offices, residences, hotels, logistics facilities, and integrated estates. While the company has evolved over the decades, many of the principles associated with its founder remain unchanged: understand people’s needs, study opportunities carefully, use resources wisely, and build with the future in mind.

BUILT TO COMMEMORATE. Bridgetowne stands as a testament to Robinsons Land’s commitment to long-term value creation, with John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard serving as the estate’s central corridor.

The buildings and destinations are the most visible part of what Mr. John helped create. Behind them is a way of thinking formed much earlier, when a young boy learned to turn hardship into opportunity and uncertainty into possibility.

Today, as Robinsons Land marks John Gokongwei Jr.’s 100th birth anniversary and the inauguration of the boulevard that now bears his name, his legacy continues to live on not only through the places that were built, but through the values that continue to guide them. For the generations who will pass through John Gokongwei Jr. Boulevard in the years ahead, it serves as a reminder that meaningful progress begins with vision, perseverance, and the courage to build for the future.

Explore the story of John Gokongwei Jr. and the values that continue to guide Robinsons Land here. – Rappler.com

World.title: eGov GPT Expansion Advances Kazakhstan’s Digital Government Push
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand its AI-powered eGov GPT assistant so that services available through it account for approximately 70% of citizen requests by the end of 2026, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at an Aug. 11 government meeting.

The assistant currently provides access to 50 of the most frequently requested government services, which together account for approximately 30% of citizen requests. Since its launch in April, eGov GPT has been used more than 150,000 times. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministry and government agencies to increase the number of services available through the assistant to 150 by year-end.

The system allows users to describe their situation in ordinary text rather than search for the appropriate form, certificate or government agency. The assistant identifies the relevant service, prepares the required application and provides the result.

“eGov GPT should become a universal AI assistant for all matters involving interaction between the state and citizens,” said Madiyev.

The expansion is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into public services under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, approved in June.

“The year of digitalization and artificial intelligence marks the starting point for achieving this goal. In June, the nationwide Digital Qazaqstan strategy was approved, with the digitalization of public services identified as one of its key priorities,” said Bektenov.

The Aug. 11 meeting, chaired by Bektenov, focused on developing an AI-based public service ecosystem and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to accelerate digital transformation across the economy and public administration. The government is also seeking to make interactions with citizens and businesses increasingly digital and proactive.

Government agencies shift to QazTech

All government agencies are now working with QazTech, Kazakhstan’s unified platform for developing digital public services, while the migration of existing information systems continues under a two-year government plan. The platform has been operating since April 1 and is designed to shorten the development and launch of new digital services from several years to several weeks.

“This year, 39 systems are scheduled for migration, with work on 36 nearing completion. Another 25 systems are being migrated or developed outside the plan, while 10 systems are already fully operational on the platform. This means the work is progressing ahead of schedule, and today all government agencies are already working with QazTech,” said Madiyev.

A moratorium on creating new government information systems outside QazTech has also been in effect since the beginning of 2026. The move is intended to consolidate digital development within a common technological environment, reduce duplicative systems and establish shared standards across government agencies.

Kazakhstan launches eGov 3.0

The government has also launched eGov 3.0, an upgraded version of Kazakhstan’s electronic government portal built on the QazTech platform.

According to Madiyev, the previous eGov portal had reached the limits of its technological capacity, prompting the launch of eGov 3.0 on the QazTech platform. The upgraded portal simplifies services by removing unnecessary requirements and steps, with several of the most frequently requested services already available in the new format.

The modernization is aimed at simplifying access to public services while reducing pressure on government digital infrastructure as demand for online services continues to grow.

According to the latest United Nations e-government survey published in 2024, Kazakhstan ranks 24th among 193 countries in the E-Government Development Index, with a score of 0.9009, placing it in the UN’s “very high” e-government development group.

World.title: What Lies Behind Kazakhstan’s External Debt
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s external debt rose 7.5% year on year to $182.8 billion as of April 1. External liabilities of the government and state-controlled institutions jumped 39%, while private-sector debt remained virtually unchanged and intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment declined 5.5% in one year.

The National Bank defines external debt as debt obligations of Kazakhstan’s residents to nonresidents. The measure covers both public- and private-sector liabilities and includes debt regardless of the currency in which it is denominated.

From April 1, 2025 to April 1, 2026, gross external debt increased from $170 billion to $182.8 billion, up $12.8 billion, or 7.5%. Intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment fell from $92.5 billion to $87.4 billion, a decline of 5.5%. As of April, $19.2 billion was owed by banks, an increase from $14.6 billion a year earlier.

Public external debt rose from $14.7 to $18.9 billion in a year. The figures show that most of Kazakhstan’s external liabilities remain outside the government balance sheet. The latest National Bank data points to sovereign and state-controlled borrowers accounting for a growing share of the increase since the start of 2025.

Kazakhstan’s external debt is predominantly long term, with 87.1% carrying an original maturity of more than one year. According to the National Bank, that limits immediate liquidity pressure, but it does not remove longer-term risks, as refinancing and servicing costs can rise when global financial conditions tighten. Loans and borrowings from nonresidents make up 69.2% of the total, while debt securities held by foreign investors account for 13%.

By creditor jurisdiction, the Netherlands accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s external debt as of April 1, at approximately $40.8 billion, followed by the United Kingdom at $19.8 billion, Russia at $16.7 billion, China at $13.8 billion and the United States at $11 billion.

The figures should not be interpreted as direct bilateral government lending, however, as they include corporate and intercompany liabilities and may reflect the jurisdiction through which financial claims are held or administered. In the case of the Netherlands, data from the National Bank shows that of $41 billion total, government debt is only $21 million, banks – $11 million and intercompany debt – $38.23 billion, so roughly 94% of Kazakhstan’s debt recorded against the Netherlands is intercompany FDI debt.

External debt of Central Asian countries excluding Turkmenistan increased by 34.9% over the past five years, reaching nearly $290.8 billion in 2025, according to data from the CIS Statistical Committee and the Eurasian Economic Commission. Kazakhstan accounted for 62.5% of the total.

Despite having by far the largest external debt stock in Central Asia, Kazakhstan’s general government debt burden remains comparatively moderate. The International Monetary Fund data put general government gross debt at around 24.9% of GDP, compared with 27.5% in Uzbekistan and 37.4% in Kyrgyzstan.

The size of the debt, however, is only one measure of fiscal vulnerability. Economists also look at the cost of servicing it, its currency and maturity structure, and how borrowed funds are used. A country with a relatively high debt ratio can remain financially stable if investors retain confidence and debt-service costs remain manageable.

World.title: New Security Architecture: Future of Abraham Accords and  Emerging Strategic Landscape for Kazakhstan
World.content:
On July 22, Washington hosted an important hearing of the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa, titled “Building a New Regional Security Architecture: The Next Phase of the Abraham Accords.” American lawmakers, diplomats, and experts, including Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel, gathered at the Capitol to discuss the broader transformation of the framework under the auspices of the White House.

The hearing, together with the current geopolitical agenda, made one trend increasingly clear: the Abraham Accords have moved decisively beyond the confines of the Middle East and are evolving into a broader international coalition, with Kazakhstan assuming an important precedent-setting role.

The discussions in Congress provide valuable insight into the key trends likely to shape the future development of the Accords and help define Astana’s place within this emerging international architecture.

Resetting the framework: From a regional pact to a “Club of Power”

Speakers before Congress emphasized that the Abraham Accords have demonstrated their resilience even under the most difficult circumstances following the October 2023 crisis. The current strategy of the Donald Trump administration rests on two major pillars.

The U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal

The long-anticipated agreement on civilian nuclear cooperation between Washington and Riyadh has now been concluded. On July 22, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed an agreement establishing a framework for long-term cooperation on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

The significance of the agreement extends well beyond the energy sector. It represents an important element of the broader U.S. strategy to build a new regional architecture in which economic integration, advanced technology, energy cooperation, and security partnerships increasingly complement the normalization process associated with the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, the nuclear agreement should be viewed separately from the question of Saudi-Israeli normalization. While normalization remains an important strategic objective for Washington, the two tracks are not identical. The conclusion of the nuclear agreement nevertheless strengthens the broader strategic framework within which future regional arrangements may develop.

Expanding the Geographic Scope

The second pillar is the expansion of the Accords beyond their original Middle Eastern framework. Bringing influential states from outside the Arab world into the process demonstrates that the platform can serve as a broader mechanism for international cooperation, reinforcing its relevance, resilience, and legitimacy.

The Central Asian dimension: why do the Accords matter for Kazakhstan?

Kazakhstan’s formal accession to the Abraham Accords in November 2025 was highlighted at the congressional hearing as an important diplomatic precedent. Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel and a prominent American expert on the regional normalization process,emphasized in his testimony that Kazakhstan’s decision helped dispel skepticism about the framework and demonstrated its appeal beyond the Arab world, particularly among moderate Muslim-majority states.

Against the backdrop of today’s geopolitical turbulence, participation in the Accords offers Kazakhstan three strategic opportunities.

Diplomatic Balancing and Multi-Vector Foreign Policy

Positioned at the intersection of Russian and Chinese interests, Astana can use the platform as an additional instrument for diversifying its international partnerships. This allows Kazakhstan to broaden its network of strategic partners without entering into direct confrontation with regional powers or Tehran.

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s engagement with the Abraham Accords should not be interpreted as a departure from its traditional multi-vector foreign policy. Rather, it reflects an adaptation of that policy to a rapidly changing global environment.

Experts increasingly point to a shift from a largely passive model of maneuvering between major powers toward a more active model of pragmatic and sovereign balancing, in which foreign policy is increasingly anchored in the protection of national interests and economic security.

Under this approach, diversification is not an end in itself. It is a strategic instrument designed to preserve Kazakhstan’s sovereignty, expand its room for maneuver, reduce excessive dependence on any single external partner, and secure access to capital, technology, markets, and critical infrastructure.

Participation in the Abraham Accords therefore fits within the broader evolution of Kazakhstan’s foreign policy: not a rejection of multi-vector diplomacy, but its modernization in response to a more fragmented, competitive, and unpredictable international system.

A Direct Track to Washington

Demonstrating support for U.S.-backed peace and normalization initiatives can strengthen Kazakhstan’s standing in Washington. This is particularly important for safeguarding long-term American investment in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and critical minerals, while also helping the country navigate the risks created by global tariff disputes and geopolitical fragmentation.

For Astana, closer engagement with the United States through emerging regional frameworks can therefore serve both diplomatic and economic purposes. It creates an additional channel for dialogue with Washington while reinforcing Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of maintaining diversified external partnerships.

A Pragmatic Economic Foundation

The expanding framework can provide Astana with access to new sources of capital and technology. Wealthy Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, can contribute financing to major infrastructure and connectivity projects, while Israel offers advanced expertise in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, water management, agricultural technology, and resource efficiency.

For Kazakhstan, therefore, the value of the Accords lies not simply in diplomatic symbolism. Their importance increasingly rests on the possibility of connecting different pools of capital, technology, infrastructure, and political influence within a broader international framework.

At the same time, as experts at the hearing made clear, Kazakhstan retains its sovereign position. Participation in the Accords does not alter Astana’s commitment to a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or its support for humanitarian efforts. Kazakhstan can therefore participate in the emerging framework while maintaining its established position on the Palestinian issue.

The future of the Abraham Accords lies in their transformation from a primarily regional political and security framework into a broader international network encompassing security, connectivity, logistics, energy, investment, and technological cooperation under U.S. leadership.

The developments of 2026 suggest that this transformation is already underway. The expansion of the Accords beyond the Arab world, Kazakhstan’s participation, and the newly concluded U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement all point toward an emerging architecture that is considerably broader than the original normalization framework.

For Kazakhstan, the Abraham Accords are therefore becoming more than a symbolic diplomatic gesture. They represent an additional instrument of the country’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy — one that can help Astana diversify strategic partnerships, attract new investment and technology, deepen its engagement with Washington and the Gulf states, and strengthen its resilience amid growing geopolitical competition.

The strategic opportunity for Kazakhstan lies in turning its early participation into practical cooperation — transforming diplomatic positioning into tangible economic benefits, technological partnerships, and greater geopolitical resilience.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, an independent think tank based at Astana International University.
