Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Wildberries warehouse ablaze, 13 killed as Russia, Ukraine trade fire
World.content:
Thirteen people have been killed and a Wildberries warehouse set ablaze as Russia and Ukraine traded attacks on Tuesday, local time.

Russian attacks killed six people and wounded 20 in the south-eastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia and also struck Kyiv, triggering fires in the capital, officials said.

Zaporizhzhia regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian troops launched missiles and aerial bombs at the city. He posted pictures showing buildings and vehicles ablaze.

Air raid alerts were sounded in both Zaporizhzhia and in Kyiv, where the capital's military administration said warehouses in a central district were ablaze. One person was reported injured.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, local authorities reported another six people were killed and 16 wounded in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk.

Ukrainian attack kills one, triggers Wildberries fire

A drone attack killed one person and injured two others in Russia's Voronezh region, while falling debris triggered fires at a Wildberries warehouse, regional governor Alexander Gusev and the company said.

North Korea benefits from Russia alliance Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Russia's air defence units destroyed 15 drones over the city of Voronezh and five districts of the region, Mr Gusev said on Telegram.

"A drone crash caused fires at two warehouses of a large company. At one facility, the fire has been contained to an area of 16,000 square metres, while at the other, a blaze covering 20,000 square metres is being extinguished. Emergency services are on scene," the governor said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Russian online retailer Wildberries said its logistics facilities in the Voronezh region had been evacuated in accordance with safety requirements.

It later said that the fire at the facility had been extinguished, that goods had not been damaged and that deliveries had been rerouted to other warehouses.

An industrial enterprise was on fire in Russia's Orenburg region after an attack by "enemy drones", the local governor said on Tuesday.

There had been no reports of casualties, Yevgeny Solntsev said.

Reuters

World.title: Luxury cruise ship passengers ferried to shore after strike closes port
World.content:
Cruise boat passengers on luxury tours of Western Australia’s remote north have been ferried to shore using tenders and provisions loaded by hand onto ships as work stoppages at Broome’s port begin to take effect.

Stevedoring and maintenance employees walked off the job last Friday after failing to reach an agreement with the Kimberley Ports Authority (KPA) over wages and conditions.

Cruise ship crew have been forced to hand load cargo and transfer passengers in small boats. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

The strike action is set to impact both of the port’s terminals for two weeks.

It's the second major industrial action in the state's north in less than a week, following unrelated work stoppages at BHP's facilities in Port Hedland over the weekend.

Small business impact

Two livestock ships and seven cruise boats were due to berth at KPA port this week, while another 12 vessels were due alongside the adjacent, privately owned floating jetty.

Discovery One Cruises owner Erie Astrup said her crews had been forced to load provisions from the slipway near the wharf, instead of relying on stevedores and cranes.

"I support the negotiations that are going on but it really does have a huge knock-on effect for the whole community, all the tourism industry, the small businesses," she said.

"And that can feel a bit unfair and challenging for many because it's a short tourism season in the Kimberley."

Discovery One has operated cruises in the Kimberley region for 26 years. (Supplied: Erle Astrup)

It is unclear how larger cruise boats, due alongside this week with up to 300 people on board, will manage the massive amount of food and fuel required for voyages.

The luxury cruiser Le Jacques Cartier had been scheduled to dock at KPA's main wharf on Tuesday morning, but remained offshore.

Passengers were seen being ferried to the slipway using the ship's tenders.

Ponant Explorations CEO Deb Corbett said the company was making the necessary arrangements to manage Le Jacques Cartier's schedule and would update its guests directly.

The luxury cruise boat Le Jacques Cartier moored offshore instead of being alongside as scheduled the Broome wharf during the strike action. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Shayne Murray, who runs a bus company which regularly services visiting cruise boats, said the transfers using the slipway were "not ideal".

"But it's working well — the tide's in our favour and the easterlies aren't in today," he said.

Industry rallies

Mr Murray is also the president of Cruise Broome, an association of industry and volunteers who help promote and manage cruise groups to the town.

"It [the strike action] affects everyone, from the hotels to planes, the people who pay a lot of money for these cruises," he said.

The tourism and livestock industries are concerned about the impact of a protracted strike at Broome port. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

In an online post, Liberal MLC Neil Thomson said it was "so embarrassing for our state to have people disembarking via the slipway rather than on the new multi-million dollar port facility".

KPA port workers and their union, the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA), have been trying to negotiate a new enterprise agreement since October last year.

Union defends strike

MUA WA branch secretary Will Tracey said the strike action was justified.

“Broome tradesmen are paid the lowest rates for tradesmen at port authorities in the state,” he said.

“The cost of living has only increased since the last agreement was done and there should be a reflection of that within the Broome area allowance, which compensates for the excessive cost of living across the Kimberley.”

The union said strike action at the port came as a last resort. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

In a statement, the KPA said it would continue to meet with employees and the union and "bargain in good faith" to resolve the outstanding items, with the Fair Work Commission now assisting in conciliation.

The parties are due to meet again tomorrow.

World.title: Why police took 20 hours to identify 'body' in suitcase as lifelike doll
World.content:
The more than 20 hours it took to establish suspected human remains found in a suitcase near Goulburn were actually a life-like doll highlights the painstaking process required to preserve a potential crime scene, according to a forensic expert.

NSW Police have revealed investigators deliberately decided to examine the bag and its contents at a mortuary rather than at the remote Oallen crime scene, to avoid potentially losing fragile forensic evidence.

Forensic expert Xanthe Weston says while it might seem extraordinary that a doll could be mistaken for a woman's body, she can understand how it happened.

"So whilst it seems that it is ridiculous almost that a doll could be mistaken for a human, I can totally see how that could have happened and the police did absolutely the right thing," Dr Weston said.

Forensic expert Dr Xanthe Weston says some modern life-like dolls can be extraordinarily realistic. (Supplied: University of Newcastle)

"Not disturbing that scene and making sure that it was not forensically relevant rather than destroying the scene, suspecting it could be a doll. So they actually followed protocol."

In a statement, police said there was "no typical time frame" for determining whether unknown remains are human because no two crime scenes are the same.

'A forensic and operational decision'

They said the Oallen discovery was treated as a suspicious death, with investigators believing a potentially decomposed body was inside a bag in remote bushland, with light and weather conditions deteriorating.

"A forensic and operational decision was made that the examination of the bag and its contents should be conducted at a mortuary with sophisticated medical and scientific equipment, to mitigate any risk of fragile forensic evidence being lost."

Dr Weston said the roughly 20-hour time frame was not extraordinary from a forensic perspective.

"I know that people will probably want to be quite critical, but from a forensic perspective, an identification perspective, this is exactly as I would have expected it to go," she said.

She said investigators faced a fundamental problem, if the suitcase did contain a homicide victim, disturbing it simply to establish what was inside could destroy evidence.

"If there is a body in there, you cannot afford to contaminate it or damage any of that evidence. So it has to be done in a very controlled, methodical way."

That could include first examining the surrounding scene and the outside of the suitcase before opening it, with Dr Weston saying fibres, hair, skin cells or DNA transfer could otherwise be lost.

"Once it's gone, all compromised, it's gone. There's no coming back from that."

Dr Weston said mistakes involving suspected human remains were not unprecedented.

She recalled working in Scotland when police were concerned remains found in an area where authorities were searching for a missing young woman were human.

She said a dog walker had gone home, returned with a plastic bag and dug up the remains before they were examined.

"They were brought in a plastic bag and it was a sheep. I was so relieved because imagine that scene was totally destroyed if they had been human remains," Dr Weston said.

'Extraordinarily convincing'

Dr Weston said modern lifelike dolls could also be extraordinarily convincing and she had professionally examined both adult and childlike dolls.

"Some of them are not at all lifelike, but some, they are becoming more and more realistic because obviously that's what the market is requesting. They want realism," she said.

She cautioned against assuming markings on the Oallen doll, which police said resembled bruises and grazes, had been deliberately designed to depict injuries.

Dr Weston said intentionally replicated bruising was not something she had encountered and the marks could have been dirt or damage interpreted as injuries, because investigators believed they were looking at human remains.

Police said the markings gave further weight to the initial belief the suitcase contained a deceased person.

But with the contents now established as non-human, police said there would be no further investigation.

NSW Police also said the response to the incident was appropriate and reports of this nature were expected to be taken seriously and managed professionally.

World.title: Billionaire Andrew Forrest scores win against Meta in scam ads case
World.content:
A US Federal court has ruled that Meta failed to preserve key evidence in an ongoing legal battle with Andrew Forrest, an outcome the Australian billionaire said could help make sure the social media giant did not "outrun responsibility".

Mr Forrest is suing Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission.

His legal team said the adverts, which show him endorsing fraudulent cryptocurrency and other investment products on Facebook, have "plagued" the mining magnate for years and duped thousands of victims.

Meta has countered that the offending marketing messages were not its doing.

Meta has said that it did not produce the scam ads, which according to the law suit, racked up thousands of victims. (Reuters: Daniel Cole/File)

In April, Australian tycoon battles Meta over fake ads which shields internet firms from being accountable for content posted by users on their platforms.

The hearing also looked into whether Meta had wrongly ditched evidence, forfeiting its ability to take shelter behind the act.

On Tuesday, the judge has found Meta had "spoliated evidence … resulting in prejudice to Forrest".

Evidence not preserved

The ruling also stated the company had failed to take reasonable steps to preserve electronically stored information that should have been kept in anticipation of litigation, including the final scam ads that were shown to victims.

Under US law, spoliation is the intentional, reckless, or negligent withholding, hiding, altering, or destroying of evidence relevant to a legal proceeding.

The ruling said in this case Meta should have foreseen the need to preserve any data relevant to the case.

Inside the scams stealing the identities of celebrities The words emblazoned across the ads are dramatic, and they're usually accompanied by a photoshopped or AI-generated image of an Australian celebrity being arrested. It's an attempt to take your money.

The ruling said if the jury found at trial that Meta acted with the intent to deprive Mr Forrest of the information, they should also assume the evidence in question was unfavourable to Meta.

'Clear message'

Mr Forrest welcomed the ruling, saying: "We now have a glimmer of hope of correcting a huge injustice inflicted on society".

Forrest's legal team has argued that Meta's artificial intelligence tools optimised and personalised fraudulent ads before distributing them. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

"Meta's conduct in this litigation so far has been evasive, duplicitous and deeply revealing. It exposes a corporate culture that disregards proper and fair process with little restraint.

"The Court's sanctions send a clear message. Meta cannot destroy or lose evidence and then use that missing evidence as a shield. The penalties for these wrongdoings must fall on Meta, not on the victims of scam advertising."

The court said Mr Forrest was entitled to fees and costs incurred as of the ruling, and that he and Meta must meet to discuss how much should be awarded.

Meta is cracking down on fake celebrity scams Financial advertisers on Facebook and Instagram will be required to reveal who is paying for the ads and who benefits from them.

Mr Forrest had previously launched criminal charges against Meta in 2022 in an Australian court, but they were discontinued in 2024.

Since 2019, thousands of deceptive s on Facebook have used the likeness of the highly prominent businessman to promote scams, racking up thousands of victims, according to the suit.

The billionaire's legal team argues that Meta's artificial intelligence tools optimised and personalised fraudulent ads before distributing them, thereby making Meta an active participant, rather than a mere intermediary.

World.title: Trump reportedly hid in catering truck to evade 'dangerous flight'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Türkiye last month when the White House said he was flying aboard Air Force One, in an extraordinary move that involved hiding him in an airport catering truck, the Washington Post reports.

Mr Trump had taken the newly renovated Qatari-donated jet to Ankara for the NATO summit but he unexpectedly used an older Air Force One when departing the country, a move that prompted questions about the newer plane's security.

The trip to NATO was the first international travel for the new plane, whose speedy upgrades triggered questions over its cost and security, and took place as hostilities escalated with Iran, which borders Türkiye.

Secret Service reportedly urged Trump to leave Türkiye on old Air Force One Officials reportedly urged the US president to swap out his Qatari-donated luxury jet as a security precaution.

Before departing Ankara, Mr Trump said on Truth Social that he would use an older baby blue Air Force One plane "for old time's sake" ⁠to RAF Mildenhall in Britain, while the new plane stopped at the same base so US service members stationed there could tour the aircraft.

After Mr Trump boarded the old Air Force One in front of cameras in Ankara, he was secretly shuttled by an airport catering truck to a smaller plane, an Air Force C-32A, the Post reported, citing a US official familiar with the operation and corroborating material it reviewed.

The deception operation was triggered by a credible Iranian assassination threat to Mr Trump, the Post reported.

A US official with knowledge of the deception plan also confirmed the operation to the New York Times.

A similar operation had taken place in 2000, when President Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as decoy.

On this occasion, the journalists who thought they were travelling with Mr Trump on the older Air Force One, which was effectively used as a decoy, reported being advised to keep their window shades in the press cabin closed.

Donald Trump boards the new, Qatari-gifted Air Force One to return to Washington at RAF Mildenhall in July 2026. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The Post said aside from reporters, some White House staff also believed that the president was on board.

When asked later by reporters why they had to keep their shades shut during the flight, Mr Trump said it was because they were "probably on a dangerous flight".

He went on to say: "But if I go, you go. Right?"

The C-32A carrying Mr Trump flew to Britain and arrived at around 10:20pm while the older Air Force One and media arrived minutes later, the Post reported.

It was not clear, the paper said, how Mr Trump was moved from the C-32A back to Air Force One.

Mr Trump's travelling press pool reported he climbed down the stairs of the old Air Force One at 10:56pm UK local time.

He gave press a peace sign but didn't walk over to talk to them. He then spent some time greeting service members before walking to the new, Qatari-donated plane.

Pictures show interior of US' new Air Force One jet The jet, gifted to the US government by Qatar, has been retrofitted, with Trump shaking off concerns over the cost.

When asked for comment on the revelation of a secret flight on a third plane, the White House provided a statement from Communications Director Steve Cheung.

He said the Qatari-donated jet has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff.

"As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," Mr Cheung said.

It was the same statement provided to the Post.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The new plane, with red, white, dark blue and gold livery chosen by Mr Trump, is a Boeing 747 gifted to the United States by Qatar last year and refitted by defence contractor L3Harris Technologies.

It was intended to serve as a temporary replacement while Boeing struggled to deliver long-delayed next-generation Air Force One planes.

Reuters

World.title: Boy, 10, clotheslined by wire on remote dirt bike track
World.content:
Ten year old Braymond Pyke had to be airlifted to hospital after injuring his neck when he rode his motorbike into a piece of rope that had been strung up across an outback Queensland dirt bike track.

His mum, Bronwyn Wood, said they were getting ready to head home late on Friday when he begged her to go for one last ride around the track just outside Cunnamulla, about 790km west of Brisbane.

Aerial of Cunnamulla, a small outback Queensland town about 790km west of Brisbane. (Supplied: Peninsula Hot Springs)

“He's like 'please mum', so of course I let him go for one more lap,” she said.

But she said she soon heard Braymond’s scream for help.

"My son was just bleeding from the throat," she said.

"It's the worst thing … you never want to imagine.

"I've never seen him in so much pain. It was horrifying.”

Braymond Pyke boarding a Royal Flying Doctor plane, and transported from Cunnamulla to Toowoomba. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

She said she drove her son straight to the Cunnamulla hospital before he was flown to Roma and on to Toowoomba Hospital for treatment.

Braymond returned home to Cunnamulla on Monday nursing severe rope burn, scratches on his neck, and some internal bruising after the clotheslining incident.

"The relief, knowing that the outcome could have been so much worse. He is one very lucky boy," Ms Wood said.

Braymond Pyke riding a motorcycle on a Cunnamulla dirt bike track. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

Ropes potentially left by drovers

Police said they are investigating the crash and have patrolled the track for any further risks.

Braymond’s dad, Brendon Pyke, said the area along Old Charleville Road had been used by drovers recently and suggested it was possible that the ropes had mistakenly been left up.

"It's electric fence wire designed to hold cattle in," he said.

"I can't say for sure but I'm thinking maybe they have left it behind."

An electric fence wire was tied up across the Bandy motorcycle track in Cunnamulla with no visible marking. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

Mr Pyke said it was drovers' responsibility to mark any ropes or wires and take them down when they were done.

He said they couldn’t confirm how the wire was left up, but also didn’t rule out that it could have been tied up by someone intentionally.

He warned families to be cautious.

Braymond Pyke's parents Bronwyn Wood and Brendon Pyke. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

"Double check where your kids are going to be riding," he said.

Cunnamulla resident Troy Nelson started to maintain the motorbike track when his own two boys started riding several years ago.

Mr Nelson and his sons found about 10 similar ropes in the area following Braymond’s injury and cut them all down.

Braymond Pyke riding a motorcycle in Cunnamulla. (Supplied: Bronwyn Wood)

He said Braymond’s injury was not the first case he had heard of recently.

“Only a couple of weeks ago, another kid actually got caught as well on a rope,” he said.

Mr Nelson said the boy had not been severely injured and decided not to report it.

World.title: Service stations nationwide raided over illegal tobacco, vapes
World.content:
More than 100 service stations across the country have been raided in a coordinated blitz targeting "suspected criminal activity" and the alleged sale of illicit tobacco and vapes.

The Australian Border Force (ABF) said nearly 300 personnel were deployed to every state and territory except Tasmania and the Northern Territory on Tuesday as part of the coordinated campaign.

Fifteen federal and state agencies were involved in Operation Shorthand, including NSW Police, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, operating under the Illicit Tobacco National Disruption Group (NDG), established by the federal government in 2025.

Australian Federal Police officers at a petrol station. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

Footage of one raid showed officers entering a service station, seizing packets of imported tobacco boxes and cash.

ABF Assistant Commissioner Customs Compliance and Enforcement Tony Smith said all agencies had a shared goal of disrupting an evolving illegal tobacco trade.

"Criminal actors are continuing to adapt their business models and diversify their activities by moving away from traditional tobacconists and in to selling their products out of convenience stores, milk bars and even service stations," he said.

"This diversification demonstrates an enforcement pressure from border agencies and our partners across the country and internationally is forcing criminal enablers to adapt their tactics to evade detection and enforcement."

The raids were nationwide except Tasmania and the NT. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

AFP Superintendent Crime Command Jim Rowe said their intelligence suggested the illegal tobacco trade was connected to organised crime.

"We have seen organised crime groups use the sales of illicit tobacco to fund further criminal activity," he said.

"The aim of today's enforcement activity for the AFP is to obtain information to help us identify the potential importation of illicit tobacco, distribution networks and how the proceeds of sales are collected and then distributed."

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said that NSW Health was were part of the multi-agency effort.

"We work closely with our federal enforcement agencies to share intelligence around people who are doing the wrong thing," he said.

"It's not fair on legitimate small business owners, it's not fair on the community or young children that these stores are popping up and are selling illegal products across the board."

The ABF said the operation remained active as NDG agencies assessed evidence gathered during the raids.

Some of the targeted service stations may be closed temporarily.

The ABC has reached out to the Australian Service Station and Convenience Store Association for comment.

World.title: Small but promising signs of recovery on Great Barrier Reef
World.content:
Monsoons spared the Great Barrier Reef from the worst heat during the 2025-26 summer allowing some coral to recover, according to a new report from the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).

"We have to place this in the context that these are small, [but] it's promising signs of recovery from the really large declines we saw from the 2024 bleaching event," said lead researcher on the long-term monitoring program, Mike Emslie.

Surveys also looked for evidence of crown-of-thorns starfish infestation as well as bleaching prevalence. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

Dr Emslie said there was a smaller bleaching event in 2025 when temperatures increased in the early part of the summer, but the onset of a monsoon brought some relief to the corals.

Hard coral cover On the Northern Great Barrier Reef, hard coral cover increased from 30 per cent to 35.1 per cent

In the Central Great Barrier Reef, hard coral cover increased from 28.6 per cent to 31.6 per cent

On the Southern Great Barrier Reef, hard coral cover decreased from 26.9 per cent to 26.4 per cent Source: AIMS

"It managed to produce a lot of cloud cover and rain and brought the sea surface temperatures down," he said.

He said this provided some relief for the corals and gave an opportunity for the organisms to start growing again.

Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority chief scientist Roger Beeden said it was an encouraging sign and showed the reef was close to the long-term average coral cover.

"We see [the reef's] inherent resilience, its ability to be able to recover when the time periods allow when there aren't so many pressures," he said.

"But the counterpoint to that is that it's under increasing pressure."

The forecast El El Niño

Dr Emslie said while it was positive showing that the reef had capacity to recover, more frequent and severe heat stress events were a growing concern.

And the forecast El El Niño could mean further stress to the reef, he said.

Scientists say the results are positive, showing the reef still has the capacity for resilience. (ABC News: Holly Richardson)

"We know from the past that El Niño events have led to widespread severe bleaching, so I guess it's a case of wait, watch and see what happens over the upcoming summer.

"We've really got to be taking very strong measures to reduce global greenhouse emissions to continue the prospects of the reef into the future."

Dr Beeden agreed it was too early to speculate on the potential impact of the El Niño event on the reef.

"It's important to note where that warmer water is concentrated at the moment is actually over the other side of the Pacific right now," he said.

" Whilst temperatures are still above the very long-term average, they're not at a point where we'd see any particular temperature driven stress on the Great Barrier Reef right now. "

He said multiple climate drivers determined outcomes in Australia's waters.

"The reality of climate change is that these kinds of events are becoming more likely: the risk of marine heat waves that can lead to coral bleaching events, coral bleaching events are a modern phenomenon," said Dr Beeden.

World.title: Howard offers a good tip about gambling reform
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Labor voter, I strangely see myself siding with former PM John Howard on gambling reform (“Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech”, August 11). Howard’s call that both major parties should act in the “public interest” should be par for the course. His statement that “If that means disappointing big companies, then disappoint them” resonates from a time when politicians prosecuted good policies such as compulsory superannuation, capital gains tax and gun control reforms, regardless of vested interests. Recent changes to housing policies, despite the bleating of some wealthy property investors, were a good start. The government must take on the bloated gambling industry and multinational gas companies if it is serious about working in the public interest, not just appeasing big business who clearly work for themselves and their shareholders, not the Australian public. Craig Jory, Albury Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former prime minister John Howard and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen, Dylan Coker In the government’s latest attempt to curb gambling advertising, PM Anthony Albanese says he wants to get the balance right between restricting gambling advertising and those who like to “have a punt on a Saturday”. This statement confuses access to gambling with its excessive promotion through advertising. Gambling is legal and any adult so inclined can easily find the gambling outlets. The concern is the power of advertising to create further demand for a product that can influence children and lead to gambling addiction. The community would be better served if gambling advertising was banned or further restricted. Leo Sorbello, Leichhardt Over-ripe Angus Taylor insists that the PM apologise to his Japanese counterpart over the “melons” reference in a podcast aired in July (“Taylor demands PM apologise to Japanese leader over ‘beautiful melons’ comment”, August 11). Cue Jane Hume and Barnaby Joyce to join in with predictably full-throated condemnation. But it didn’t occur to any of them at the time. The pearl-clutching only happened after the matter was raised weeks after the event by the Japanese ambassador, and Taylor et al saw it as an excuse to have yet another go. With so little of their own to talk about that matters, I guess all they’re left with is mock-pious indignation about stuff that doesn’t. Adrian Connelly, Springwood You know it’s going to be a difficult day when you have to agree with Angus Taylor and Barnaby Joyce (“Takaichi will brush off melon joke. She shouldn’t have to”, August 11). What was Anthony Albanese thinking when he agreed to appear on the Deep Bush podcast, where he proceeded to diminish himself and humiliate this county? Fifteen-year-old boys don’t vote, so he can’t have thought it was a vote catcher. Tanya Plibersek shouldn’t have had to mount a case to defend his indefensible behaviour. Party loyalty gone a step too far, methinks. Lyn Savage, Coogee Having seen some parts of the Bush Deep podcast, I think Angus Taylor has totally misrepresented the prime minister’s remarks. In fact, the only thing that I find outrageous is that the PM actually appeared on a podcast like that. Whoever suggested that it would be a good idea should lose their job. And in future the PM might also consider avoiding podcasts by the likes of Kyle Sandilands and Karl Stefanovic. Caroline Davies, Annandale



Sign language Strathfield Council wants to mandate English shop signs to “foster unity” (“Sydney council plans to make English compulsory for all shop signs”, August 11). But unity isn’t fostered by telling 73 per cent of residents their languages rank second. Liberal councillor Esther Kim says English is “our common language”, but it’s not. In Strathfield, it’s “a common language”. That’s not a failure of integration, that’s a feature. Yet the council voted 4-2 to regulate signs that business owners say aren’t causing problems, at a cost nobody’s calculated, using rules that don’t yet exist. This isn’t policy, it’s pure theatre. It proves that you can’t legislate unity. You can only legislate conformity – and hope nobody notices the difference. Raj Kamath, Castle Hill Strathfield council passed a motion, making it compulsory for all businesses in the LGA to clearly display English on all signage. Wolter Peeters One can only wonder where Strathfield Council’s proposal might lead. We would need to abandon “restaurant”, “cafe” and “bistro” (French), “pizzeria” (Italian), “delicatessen” (German) and “kiosk” (Turkish, ultimately Persian). Then there’s “salon” and “depot” (French), “emporium” (Latin), “galeria” (Spanish), “casa” (Italian/Spanish/Portuguese), “spa” (Belgian), oh, and “bric-a-brac” and “antiques” (French again). We would also need to remove “manicure” and “pedicure” (French) and of course “kebab” (Persian). Sheesh, I need a “sedative” (Latin) just thinking about it. Ross Duncan, Potts Point Judgment I cannot believe Chris Minns decided not only to appear on Kyle Sandilands’ new show, but also to cut the ribbon (“A premier, a psychic and Pauline Hanson join Kyle Sandilands for debut”, August 11). Mr Minns, you just gave this excuse for a broadcaster legitimacy and credibility. According to Sandilands, the prime minister was also supposed to call in but thankfully never did. The premier has shown poor judgment. Doesn’t he read the papers? Tim Douglas, Hurlstone Park Medical reality



Pauline Hanson says Australian workers are lazy. She then says migration is the reason “why hospitals are turning away sick people” (“Hanson hits out at Burke on migration numbers”, August 10). Given that a large proportion of nurses and doctors in our hospitals are migrants or the children of migrants, who will keep our health system running if we don’t have adequate migration? By her definition, lazy Australians won’t be able to fit the bill. Hanson says she will “go around Australia” gathering wish lists, asking people what they want. She says she will “even visit a few fish and chip shops” to get their requests. If she visits me, I will ask her to pop out of her plane and take a walk with me through the wards and theatres of Gosford Hospital to meet some of the staff. Then I’ll ask her to get real. Bernie Bourke, Ourimbah WILCOX TOON Thinking inside the Square The artist’s impressions of the proposed Town Hall Square say it all: it’s a vanity project poorly thought out and designed (“First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square”, August 11). The square is dominated by a Victorian fountain, the dark pavement portends a heat trap, the tree types provide poor shade and shed limbs. Rather than an open space for the people, it looks like an opportunity for al fresco dining and a corporate pavilion. Ironically, the square is cut off from the Town Hall by the city’s last great project, the George Street tram, a reminder of cost blowouts, prolonged time scales and disruption. What’s missing in the picture is the last proposed vanity project, the Cloud Arch, the throwaway bikes and Sydney’s famous homeless citizens. Please, Clover, spend the money on social housing instead. Bruce McGarity, Bathurst Good thinking, Clover Moore. There is no doubt that this is a very bland corner of the city. No current building has any merit, so the bulldozers can’t come quickly enough. The Town Hall needs to finally take centre stage, and clearing the space opposite seems like a good start. I hope we aren’t still only talking about this plan in five years’ time – like the permanent outdoor music bowl in the Domain area, a William Street boulevard or the reimagined Circular Quay. Let’s hope that the city council can get started on a midtown vision to show what’s possible. Greg Vale, Kiama An artist’s impression of the proposed square opposite Sydney’s Town Hall. Choi Render Eucalypts in the square in front of the Sydney Town Hall? Surely a species of native tree more appropriate to this setting can be used. Lilly-pilly and blueberry ash come to mind, and I am sure there are others. Eucalyptus trees are known for dropping large amounts of leaf litter and branches around them to prevent other plants growing nearby. The sudden branch falls are hazardous and the oils in leaves can stain footpaths. The shade provided in summer is dappled at best. This oversimplified reference to a romanticised bushland heritage seems lazy. John Perry, Newtown



Copycat problem-solving As a former teacher of HSC students I can affirm that plagiarism is an old problem (Letters, August 11). Ethics isn’t a major concern for many students – marks are their focus, and also for their parents. One good way of sorting out those who think and evaluate for themselves is making it a requirement that footnotes and bibliographies are used. This must be taught and insisted on in hand-in assessment tasks. Students will always look for shortcuts and share with their friends, and teachers have limited time to sort out where this is occurring. Fewer take-home assessment tasks helps sort some problems out but it doesn’t promote research skills and the critical evaluation of evidence. Vivienne Parsons, Thornleigh Unhealthy system Bulk billing has climbed to 84.1 per cent but, as the Herald reports, growth has lagged for older patients whose consultations are typically longer and more complex. That detail deserves more than a passing sentence (“Free GP visits on the rise as 1400 clinics ditch out-of-pocket fees”, August 11). The bulk-billing rate is a ratio of bulk-billed attendances to all attendances. The measure counts only the consultations that happened and says nothing about the ones that didn’t – the appointments never offered because a doctor cut their hours, retired early or left the practice. So the measure can improve while the amount of care given actually decreases. If the GPs who leave are disproportionately those who charged a gap in order to run long appointments, their departure lifts the rate more. Nor does 84 per cent of attendances mean 84 per cent of all patients. Fewer than half of Australians were bulk-billed for every visit last year. A rate counts services, not people. Affordability is a price measure and we are reading it as an access measure. A free appointment you cannot get is not a health system. Dr Elly Goodsall, Newcastle Tech worth its salt On the contrary, Dennis Bluth, more solar and wind farms can provide cheap power to run more reverse osmosis desalinators (Letters, August 11). Instead of building more dams to harvest more water despite declining rainfall, as you suggest, we should be using abundant seawater to add to the environment. It could even pay for itself via expanded agricultural output if it were put in the right place. For example, a cluster of 250-gigalitre desalinators built near Port Pirie in South Australia could pump water into pipelines to Bourke via Broken Hill, which would drought-proof most of the Murray-Darling basin by adding a teralitre to the river flow. Alan Stanley, Upper Corindi Dennis Bluth urges the construction of more dams as an aspect of climate change adaptation and contends that no additional water reserves have been secured for 40 years. Well, they have, in the form of the desalination plant completed in 2010. For more dams to be constructed, watercourses and land will be submerged. Destruction of environment was the primary reason for plans to raise Warragamba Dam wall being shelved in 2023. Kate Lumley, Hurlstone Park



Safety check In the many media reports about the recent near-collisions at Sydney Airport we have had comments and criticisms from the chief executives of Airservices Australia, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, Airlines for Australia and New Zealand, the Australian Travel Industry Association and others (“Air traffic agency warned over Sydney Airport chaos”, August 11). Among all these groups and their highly paid executives, one wonders who is actually responsible for the safety of passengers, staff and airlines? Rob Phillips, North Epping Base liabilities As Peter Hartcher points out, the US bases in the Middle East were once thought to be protective assets for the host countries but in fact have turned out to be liabilities (“Middle East may be entering a post-American era”, August 11). Lessons for Australia? Richard Tainsh, Potts Point Now that America has basically lost the war in the Middle East and couldn’t even defend their Gulf State allies (as well as Ukraine), what on earth is the point of AUKUS? Tony Lewis, Mount Victoria New role model Amidst the obfuscation, the rampant memory losses, the multiple pleas of “I can’t recall” Peggy Dwyer SC maintains grace, professionalism and cool in the face of the utterly non-sensical answers being offered by the witnesses at Operation Rosny. Ms Dwyer is my new role model. Anthony Frazer, Camperdown

World.title: ‘Devil will be in the detail’: Labor under pressure to unmask accused criminals
World.content:
Updated PoliticsVictoriaCourts ‘Devil will be in the detail’: Labor under pressure to unmask accused criminals Kieran Rooney and Erin Pearson Updated August 11, 2026 — 6:03pm ,first published 11:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Convicted rapists would no longer be able to hide their identity through suppression orders designed to protect victims if Labor is re-elected in November, a move welcomed by open justice advocates who nonetheless say broader reforms are required. The state government’s change – to be legislated after the election – represents a first step towards addressing concerns with suppression orders raised by media groups and highlighted by multiple high-profile cases in which alleged abusers have succeeded in remaining unnamed on mental health grounds. Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny and Premier Ben Carroll on Tuesday. AAP Premier Ben Carroll and Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny announced the commitment on Tuesday as they introduced legislation aimed at protecting victims of abuse, including restrictions on character references and a new standalone offence for coercive control. Carroll said Labor would amend the Open Courts Act to limit the use of suppression orders in the next term of parliament. As well as barring convicted rapists from using legal manoeuvres to hide their identities, the government also flagged it could wind back the use of suppression orders for those facing criminal trials, amid an ongoing review into the use of suppression orders.



Related Article Exclusive

Press freedom Court secrecy rules to be reviewed over suppression order complaints The Age revealed in June that Kilkenny had tasked the Department of Justice and Community Safety with this review work and to consult the courts, lawyers and the media. Limiting suppression orders for convicted rapists represents a fraction of the problem. Many of the high-profile cases that have shown flaws in the system – including Ralph Carr and Tom Silvagni – have used secrecy provisions to protect the identity of those on trial. Justin Quill, partner at top-tier law firm Thomsons, said the system was broken and reforms were a “no-brainer”. “The devil will be in the detail, and until we see that detail, it’s hard to know whether the government’s announced commitment is a real one or just one that’s being said for political purposes ahead of an election in November,” he said.



Quill said convicted offenders were not the key issue, and the biggest problem with the current system was the secrecy orders that could last for years while court proceedings were under way. “We’ve got to have openness and transparency in our judicial system from start to finish, not just after someone is convicted,” he said. Lawyers regularly rely on a clause in the Open Courts Act which allows suppression orders to be considered “to protect the safety of any person”, and the government is under pressure to address this element of the legislation. The use of mental health grounds under this clause to secure suppression orders has come under increased scrutiny in recent years, particularly after being used in the 2025 rape trial of Silvagni, a member of a famous footballing family.



Silvagni’s name was suppressed during criminal proceedings after a judge accepted publicity about his case would risk harming his mental health. Major media groups, including The Age, campaigned in March alongside victims of crime to change current legislation to make it harder to obtain suppression orders on mental health grounds. Kilkenny on Tuesday said the review would aim to close any loopholes being exploited. “Justice must be open, and there must be a balance with the right to a fair trial,” she said. “But we have seen most recently that we need to look at this. We need to listen.” The Coalition, if elected, has already vowed to restrict suppression orders to genuine physical safety reasons.



Melbourne Press Club president Michael Bachelard, who is also a journalist for The Age, said the government’s announcement was welcomed but limited and light on detail. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted “The government and opposition should commit before the election to a much broader review into the law governing cases in Victoria, including the test that must be met before a suppression order is granted,” he said. “As they stand, these laws make it far too difficult in this state to keep the public informed.” For three years, Carr, 66, was on bail while he fought allegations that he raped a young woman at his Melbourne home. But the music producer did so under the cloak of anonymity. This was thanks to a wide-ranging suppression order that banned media from reporting his name, age and the industry he worked in, and from publishing pixelated photographs.



Even after a jury found him guilty of rape and sexual assault, he persisted with his suppression fight, arguing his psychological safety would be at significant risk if “public identification” occurred, before abandoning it last week. In June, this masthead revealed almost 500 suppression orders in various forms were issued in Victorian courts last year, with the highest number being issued on safety grounds – including for mental health reasons. Of those granted, 247 were made in the County Court. Last week, this masthead unmasked the identity of a doctor accused of filming women and children using showers at Melbourne public pools after fighting a suppression order sought on psychological safety grounds for the accused man’s son. He was granted a three-month interim suppression order to give lawyers time to gather evidence, despite the legislation stating these types of applications must be brought back before the court for determination as a “matter of urgency”. Melbourne University academic and lawyer Jason Bosland said: “Suppression orders that are made in circumstances that do not meet community expectations have a corrosive effect on such confidence and ultimately undermine the rule of law.”



The Carroll government also introduced a bill to parliament on Tuesday with a range of protections for victims of abuse. It included the introduction of coercive control as a standalone criminal offence, delivering on a commitment from 2025, and the removal of “good character” references which can be used to argue for lighter sentences. Harrison James has welcomed the abolition of good character references in Victoria. Riccardo Raiti Harrison James, a survivor of child sexual abuse and co-founder of the “Your Reference Ain’t Relevant” advocacy group, said character references had already been abolished in the ACT and NSW. “Good character is the very tool perpetrators use to ingratiate themselves into the lives of their victims, their families and their communities,” he said.



Related Article Justice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused “When we allow them to use that to reduce their sentence, we risk giving an offender a discount for the very thing that helped facilitate the crime.” The standalone offence of coercive control will take effect in March 2028 to provide time for an advisory group to consult on how it will be implemented. Katie Alexander, a member of the state’s Victim Survivors’ Advisory Council, said the area was so complex that a one-size-fits-all approach would not work. She said coercive control devastated her life and destroyed her family.



“It messed with my mind. It broke my body and it shattered my relationships,” Alexander said. “Repeated acts of abuse over many years have deep psychological, emotional, social and financial scars.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said her first act as Coalition leader had been to move legislation on coercive control, which was not supported by Labor at the time. “Coercive control is an insidious form of abuse and can affect anyone, but we know women are overwhelmingly the victims of intimate partner violence,” she said. “Protecting women and victim-survivors from abuse should never be political. We will always stand on the side of victim-survivors.” Other protections to be introduced include amendments to family violence intervention orders that reduce the need for victims to return to court for extensions and requiring courts to consider their views when making decisions on these extensions.



Personal safety intervention orders will also recognise grooming for the first time and fine exemptions will be extended to stop fees and charges being weaponised against victims of abuse. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Price hopes Canterbury return can start Monte Veebee on road to riches
World.content:
There’s no shortage of lucrative options in the back of co-trainer Luke Price’s mind for consistent galloper Monte Veebee beyond his return in the Chase The Dream Handicap (1250m) at Canterbury today.

It’s been a case of musical trainers for the five-year-old, who started out with the Robert and Luke Price team at Kembla but switched to the Bjorn Baker stable for his last campaign where he recorded a first-up provincial win and four city placings before coming back home.

Trainer Luke Price saddles up Monte Veebee at Canterbury on Wednesday evening. Getty Images

Price feels Monte Veebee could be an ideal horse to aim at the rich Provincial-Midway Championships series in the autumn, with its $1 million final, given he is eligible having come back to their stable well before the cut-off.

“He could be a good Four Pillars horse, too, but I hope his benchmark goes beyond that,” Price said. “I think we’ve got a city class horse back. It’s a good starting point and let’s hope he can start off like he did last prep.”

World.title: Race-by-race preview and tips for Wednesday’s Canterbury meeting
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Wednesday’s Canterbury meeting Ray Hickson August 11, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Selections based on a good to soft track. Race 1 2. Lorax put the writing on the wall with a strong first-up placing at Randwick, hitting the line from near last into third. With the extra 100m perhaps he can be a bit closer in the run. Hard to beat. 1. Threads was placed in the Black Opal earlier in the year, he may have been in need of the run when fourth behind Sequinned two weeks ago. Open to improvement. 7. Savagram took a bit of winding up in his latest trial when running into second over 1045m. Race day can be different, he’s drawn well and would be keeping him safe.

How to play it: Lorax WIN. Racing returns to Canterbury on Wednesday. Getty Images Race 2



2. Sing Your Song showed a lot of promise on debut back in April running on from well back into second behind Moscatel at 1100m. Nothing wrong with her two trials leading in, somewhat typical for the stable, she’s drawn to have every chance first-up. 1. Wanda’s Spark is the logical horse to beat with the race fitness from her debut second at Kensington two weeks ago. Hard to run down. 4. Caloocan Beauty started in the market at her only start back in January running a fair fourth. Won both trials leading in and while drawn wide she’d be a good chance with any luck.

How to play it: Sing Your Song WIN. Race 3 1. Cheval De Bois is entitled to go close on the back of three seconds on end including a handy one in BM78 grade at Rosehill last time. Obviously rising sharply in the weights for the class drop but draws ideally for his racing style and this could be his race. 3. Sister Daae is now up to 18 starts for one win but she’s racking up the placings of late and her effort to run into third last week behind a runaway leader was sound. First try this trip and is a threat. 11. Kumbaya broke through at Wyong at a mile then consolidated with a placing at Canterbury last week just back a notch in trip. Was placed over this trip earlier in the year. In the mix.

How to play it: Cheval De Bois WIN. Race 4 2. Oakfield Neptune wasn’t able to be ridden to her strengths when back to 1100m in a fast race won by Sir Les at Randwick. Previous form when right on pace at this sort of distance was excellent at the provincials and good chance to bounce back. 8. Overtook had to go back from a wide barrier at Canterbury a few weeks ago and was never in the hunt. Big barrier switch for her and down in the weights as she clicks up in class. Could surprise. 4. Kakadu Sunset resumes with blinkers on first time. Showed some ability last season with a debut win and a few placings and well worth including.

How to play it: Oakfield Neptune WIN.



Race 5 2. Monte Veebee rarely puts in a bad one and was a big winner first-up last preparation before measuring up in BM78 grade. Looks to have come up well, has a racing style that sees him right up on the speed and sure to be competitive. 8. Capture Me chased home Jarrito when coming off a six week break then scored as a $1.12 chance on the Illawarra Grange track where he was too good once the gap came. Sure to take beating. 10. Unstopabull tends to get back and run on and he did that when third behind Watson and Clear Proof three weeks ago. Has that inside gate where he’ll do no work and will be hitting the line strongly again.

How to play it: Monte Veebee EACH-WAY. Related Article Horse racing Price hopes Canterbury return can start Monte Veebee on road to riches Race 6 1. Inoue blew the starts badly at his first run for the stable but was able to overcome it and race away to a big win over this track at trip a month ago. Similar sort of race, up 3kg so won’t want to be missing the start this time. Hard to beat all things being equal. 3. Zale is racing consistently and he was run down by Inoue in that race after being on speed as usual. You know what you get with him and he can give a sight. 5. Miss Trentino is an interesting runner resuming from almost a year off the scene since winning at this track in September. Won a couple of recent trials and has the inside gate.

How to play it: Inoue WIN.



Race 7 2. Anthracite showed he’s on the right track with a handy placing at Kensington first-up two weeks ago. No support for him that day but he ran well and can only be fitter. Draws okay and the extra ground appears to suit. Have to trust him but signs are promising. 3. Barking Mad measured up quite well when chasing home Funshow at Rosehill to back up a couple of wins in Victoria. Only has to hold that form to be right in the finish. 5. Forecaster likes to lead and held on well when runner-up to Champagne Hero at Kensington a couple of weeks back. If he finds the front with a bit in hand he could give a kick.

How to play it: Anthracite WIN. BEST BETS

Race 3: (1) Cheval De Bois

Race 4: (2) Oakfield Neptune Best Value

Race 5: (2) Monte Veebee Supplied by Racing NSW

World.title: Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis
World.content:
RBA governor Michele Bullock has warned the bank is willing to keep raising interest rates to curb inflation while flagging property prices could fall by 20 per cent without seriously risking the country’s financial stability. The decision followed a warning from ANZ economists that property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes. House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao In a press conference on Tuesday, Bullock said the downturn in the property market was “not a massive risk” to financial stability, not a major factor keeping interest rates on hold, and “not [currently] the main game” for the bank. “We’ve done a little bit of work on [the property market] from a financial stability perspective,” she said. “If property prices fell by 20 per cent, still only about 5 per cent of households would be in negative equity.



“Awful circumstances [for the homeowners affected], which are compounded by the fact that you’d have to sell your house, but it doesn’t pose a risk to the financial institutions because they are very well capitalised.” On Tuesday, the bank kept the official cash rate on hold at 4.35 per cent – the same rate it set for all of 2024 – while releasing updated forecasts that showed inflation staying above the 2 to 3 per cent target band until the end of 2027. Financial markets believe there is a 50-50 chance of a further rate rise late in the year, with rate relief not expected before the second half of 2027. Bullock said the decision to keep interest rates on hold was unanimous, that a rate cut was not discussed, and that the board remained focused on ensuring high inflation did not become entrenched.



“We’ve already raised [rates] three times, and we will go again if we need to,” Bullock said. “I think personally that it’s quite possible we might need to go, but we’ll wait and see what the data tells us. Editor's pick Census Completing the census is compulsory. Skipping it can result in a hefty fine The board said in its report: “Following three increases in the cash-rate target since the beginning of the year, financial conditions are now tighter than they were, and the economy appears to be slowing as expected … But inflation is still too high.” Inflation is likely to remain high for some time, the bank warned, because of the disruption to global oil supply caused by the Iran war that meant higher fuel prices were flowing through to other goods and services. Bullock also said there was a risk that the AI-driven data centre boom in Australia could put pressure on areas such as construction, which is already facing high demand, possibly keeping inflation elevated before the nation sees any productivity improvements from the technology.



The bank said while household consumption had eased gradually, business investment had been much stronger than expected, largely driven by data centre construction. The board “will still need to see some further progress before [it] can be confident that we are going to get inflation back to target with current monetary policy settings,” Bullock said. Loading The bank’s latest forecasts show it expects economic growth to be slightly stronger, though still lacklustre, for the rest of the year compared to its forecasts in May, coming in at 1.4 per cent by Christmas and 1.6 per cent by December next year. Price growth across the economy remains above the RBA’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent, at 3.8 per cent in June, but the inflation figures were substantially lower than the 4.8 per cent figure the RBA forecast in May.



Unemployment, at 4.4 per cent in June, is still outside the rate the bank considers “full employment”. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow Treasurer Jim Chalmers told parliament the Reserve Bank’s decision to keep interest rates steady would “come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage”. “This decision reflects the fact that inflation has been coming in well under the Reserve Bank and Treasury forecasts,” Chalmers said. Earlier on Tuesday, ANZ said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year.



Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough. Related Article Exclusive

Property prices Teal MPs’ electorates are where house values are falling most. They think it’s a good thing The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak. Prices in both cities are expected to recover by almost 5 per cent in 2028. ANZ senior economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said the market was slowing sooner than they had expected due to a combination of restrictive interest rates, tax policy changes and global uncertainty. “Auction clearance rates are very soft, coming in below 50 per cent for the past 10 weeks across the capitals,” they said. World.title: RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalInterest rates RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow Shane Wright August 11, 2026 — 5:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Reserve Bank is making a lot of noise that it could lift interest rates. But the RBA’s own forecasts and analysis suggest that barring another unexpected inflation spike – the world’s looking at you, Donald Trump – it is going to struggle to follow through with that threat. RBA governor Michele Bullock on Tuesday. Brent Lewin While governor Michele Bullock often says the Reserve only has one lever to deal with inflation, she actually has another. And she deploys it every time she stands up to do a press conference or make public statements. Her voice is a powerful one. If she were to warn of economic disaster or bright days ahead, consumers, investors and markets would listen and act. In central bank jargon, it’s called jawboning.



And threatening to inflict more interest pain on the economy is a good example of jawboning. Again and again on Tuesday, she said there were upside risks to inflation and that the bank may have to tighten monetary policy further. But compare her words with the bank’s forecasts released with the decision to leave the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent. Loading The bank thinks inflation is going to be lower than it had expected. Unemployment is going to be a tad higher than it had forecast. Wages growth is a little softer. That’s all before the RBA gets a firm grip on what its previous rate rises and the federal government’s changes to property taxes – and the fallout from higher oil prices on consumer sentiment – are doing to house prices.



As the bank knows, house prices are a key swing factor in the strength of consumer spending. “Lower housing prices weigh on household consumption by reducing household net wealth and spending related to housing turnover. Weaker housing prices also reduce the incentive to build new homes,” it said. Where do the bank’s biggest inflationary threats lie? In household spending and in housing construction costs. The bank sliced its household spending forecasts, and it really cut its expectations for housing investment. In May, it thought spending on new homes would have grown by 2 per cent by year’s end. Now it thinks it’s going to contract by 0.7 per cent. Good luck to builders trying to pass on higher costs to prospective home owners when the RBA thinks there will be fewer of them.



The rates decision was announced as ANZ went the full bear on the Australian property market, predicting a peak to trough in housing prices of more than 10 per cent. In Sydney, the nation’s capital when it comes to property fascination and prices, the drop is tipped to be closer to 15 per cent. Related Article Updated

Property prices Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis Bullock finished her press conference by saying if the bank believed it would be wrong on its inflation forecasts, then it would act. As the great central banker of Springfield, Homer Simpson, would say: D’oh! Analysts assumed she was talking about its inflation forecasts being too dovish. But the bank got its last inflation forecast wrong. Instead of it being 4.8 per cent to June, it was 3.8 per cent.



Missed it by the side of a barn, really. There were good reasons for the miss – petrol prices have not soared nearly as high as feared – but it was still a long way out. And it missed its underlying inflation forecast. And it missed its unemployment forecast. And it downgraded its wage growth forecast. There’s nothing wrong with Bullock using her central bank pulpit to talk up the threat of a rate rise. It’s an important part of her armoury and one that has been tried and tested. In some ways, it can work better than a rate rise, without some of the collateral economic damage. But with previous rate rises still yet to fully work their way through the economy, and the federal government’s property tax changes taking the wind out of the national housing Ponzi scheme, something from left field will have to emerge to force Bullock to follow through with her threat.
