World.title: ‘Like he’d seen a ghost’: Ex-girlfriend says former teen athlete confided in her about Alan Jones
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former teen athlete who was allegedly indecently assaulted by Alan Jones looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he confided in his then girlfriend that the veteran broadcaster had been touching him inappropriately, a court has heard. The ex-girlfriend of complainant “J”, one of six men who has accused Jones of unwanted kissing and touching, told Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial on Tuesday that “J” swore her to secrecy after telling her about the alleged assaults. Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy “He was really uncomfortable with telling me. He had his head down,” she said.



“He did sort of aggressively [say], ‘you cannot tell anybody about this’. It was, ‘you can’t repeat it’ or, ‘you’ve got to keep it to yourself’, it was along the lines of that.” She told the Downing Centre Local Court that “J” made the disclosure during a late-night conversation in her parents’ loungeroom in the mid-2000s. He had arrived from Jones’ southern NSW property looking “emotionless” and like he had “seen a ghost”, she said. “I remember his face very clearly in my mind, and it still is very clear in my mind,” she said. He told her that “Alan Jones has touched me inappropriately”, she said.



She said “J” was not his normal self and was not looking her in the eye. She suggested to him that “maybe you want to report it” and he responded firmly, “No”, she told the court. ‘Tell my truth’ Years later, after Jones was arrested in 2024, she said “J” contacted her by text message, and they spoke later that night. “J” told her that “I’d like to come forward and tell my truth”, she said. She responded that she thought this was important, the court heard, and that “I remember you telling me all those years ago”. Complainant “J” was the first witness to give evidence in the former broadcaster’s lengthy criminal trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent.



Related Article Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Court hears brother of complainant ‘J’ received gifts from 2GB broadcaster as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues He alleges Jones kissed him and touched his penis without his consent. On the Crown’s case, the alleged assaults took place in the early 2000s when “J” was aged between 17 and 19. The former broadcaster vehemently denies wrongdoing and is defending the charges. Of the 22 charges, nine counts of indecent assault relate to “J”, who completed his evidence on Tuesday. A further five complainants will give evidence in the trial. Jones’ gifts to family of ‘J’



The brother of complainant “J” told the court on Tuesday that the then broadcaster had not only given his brother a series of gifts but had also bought him expensive presents. He said “J” had told him that “Alan would like to help out” with an engagement ring when he was planning to propose to his now wife. Jones had also bought the couple a Villeroy & Boch dinner set as a wedding gift, “J”’s brother told the court. Under cross-examination by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, he said he did not recall other gifts, after Bashir asked about a dishwasher for the family home, flowers for their mother and hampers. The brother of “J” said he was aware that Jones had given his brother a series of gifts including a mobile phone, a car, and a weekly allowance of hundreds of dollars. Records tendered in court suggest “J” received the phone about a month after his 18th birthday and the car when he was 19.



The brother told the court that “J” confided in him about the alleged indecent assaults after Jones’ arrest in November 2024. “J” had asked to meet him at a nearby McDonald’s, he told the court, and had said: “This is the hardest thing that I’ve ever had to tell you. You’ve probably seen the news about the defendant. “I’m one of the people who has come forward.” He said he asked “J” why he hadn’t told him earlier and “J” had replied that it was hard for him and he didn’t know what to do. “J” said he didn’t want “the money, the support” from Jones to stop, his brother said. He said he asked “J” how bad it had been and “J” had replied: “Nothing too bad. He didn’t try to f--- me or anything like that. He would try, he would grab me on the c---, he would kiss me … the hugs would go for longer.”



Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones’ front-row view as graphic details of alleged indecent assault are exposed Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, if he had witnessed Jones act inappropriately towards “J”, his brother said: “I didn’t.” Earlier on Tuesday, “J” was asked about texts with his former partner as he was re-examined by Wright during his sixth day of evidence. The complainant had told the court he confided in his then-girlfriend about the allegations. Last week, “J” was taken to texts exchanged with the woman after she went to police to make a statement while detectives were investigating accusations related to “J”. In those 2024 texts, he told the woman he would look after her “after it is all over”, referring to the court proceedings. Bashir suggested he was referring to financial support.



The woman wrote that speaking to police “brought back a lot” and that she didn’t remember some of it. “J” responded: “That’s great news, thank you. I didn’t want to discuss anything, so everything was all from what you remembered. I appreciate you meeting with him and providing a statement.” “J” wrote that when it was “all over” they could meet up, and he could tell her his story. The complainant denied he was alluding to financial support when he said he’d look after her, saying he was talking about her difficult sobriety journey. “I anticipated she’d have to go to court … I was grateful if she’d remembered anything,” he said.



“I was just going to support her to do that for me.” The man was also asked during re-examination by Wright why he had lied to his mother when he spoke with her following media coverage of the allegations against Jones in late 2023. The court heard he told her Jones had never touched him. He said he felt that she would have pushed him to come forward to police if he had told her. “I thought I would be called a liar and crushed in court and no one would believe me,” he said. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Labor MP took donations from club with pokies, reports himself to watchdog
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWPolitical donations Labor MP took donations from club with pokies, reports himself to watchdog Patrick Begley August 11, 2026 — 5:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A NSW Labor politician accepted thousands of dollars from a club with poker machines after the Minns government banned political donations from clubs involved in gambling. Records show Campbelltown MP Greg Warren received donations from the NSW Harness Racing Club in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Campbelltown MP Greg Warren said the harness racing club had declared it was not a prohibited donor. Greg Warren MP website The payments were made at fundraising lunch events hosted for Warren, which have featured Premier Chris Minns and Treasurer Daniel Mookhey. Following questions from this masthead, Warren said he had accepted the money “in good faith” but he would refer the payments to the electoral watchdog for assessment.



NSW, which has more poker machines than any other state or territory, closed a donations law “loophole” in 2023 by expanding the definition of gambling entity to include not-for-profit clubs with an involvement in gambling. “It is common sense,” Minns said at the time. “If other gambling entities are banned from making political donations, it should apply to all clubs.” Soon after the ban took effect, Warren held a corporate lunch attended by Minns at which the NSW Harness Racing Club contributed $3000, electoral records show. The NSW government closed a “loophole” in 2023 by banning not-for-profit clubs involved in gambling from making political donations. Peter Braig Warren recorded a $1500 donation from the club at a “Daniel Mookhey lunch” in 2024 and a further $1500 last year.



Trading as Club Menangle, the organisation operates a major racetrack south-west of Sydney, “home to the iconic Miracle Mile and the world’s richest harness race, The TAB Eureka”. It also runs the Menangle Country Club, which boasts an award-winning restaurant, picturesque garden and historic setting. Related Article Poker machines Second mega-club in firing line over dirty cash claims The venues have 50 poker machines, according to the most recent state records. Each year, the club’s accounts record poker machine revenue and commissions received from Keno and TAB sales. But most revenue comes from “TAB and wagering distributions” received from betting operators for putting on the race events. Registered clubs are banned from making political donations “if the business undertaken by the registered club includes wagering, betting, or other gambling”. It is a criminal offence to knowingly receive a prohibited donation.



Warren said the club had declared it was not prohibited. The Menangle Country Club, one of the venues operated by the NSW Harness Racing Club. Menangle Country Club “The donations were accepted in good faith with the required non-prohibited donor declaration, and were fully disclosed as per the required rules,” Warren said in a statement. “I take the required obligations under the Electoral Funding Act seriously, and have therefore taken the appropriate action for the donations to be referred to the NSW Electoral Commission for review.” Club chief executive Bruce Christison was unavailable to answer questions for medical reasons, a club spokeswoman said.



“The club has completed the political donations questionnaires honestly and transparently,” the spokeswoman said. Related Article Exclusive

Poker machines The battle over pokies comes to premier’s backyard “To ensure there is not an issue with our eligibility, we have contacted the electoral commission this morning and supplied all the relevant details and are now awaiting their response.” The NSW Electoral Commission declined to answer detailed questions, including whether the NSW Harness Racing Club met the definition of prohibited donor. The premier has faced significant pressure from within his own party to curb the problem gambling harm caused by poker machines, this masthead revealed in May.



On Monday, Minns told the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing that the government was considering pokies reforms ahead of the next election, saying “it’s clearly doing harm in the community”. A report by the NSW Audit Office last year found the regulation of pokies was “not supporting harm minimisation outcomes effectively”. World.title: Dragons recruit Koloamatangi set to make huge sacrifice for new club
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Dragons recruit Koloamatangi set to make huge sacrifice for new club Christian Nicolussi August 11, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St George Illawarra recruit Keaon Koloamatangi is considering skipping the World Cup to undergo surgery and ensure he is fit for day one of pre-season training with his new club. Koloamatangi played in all three Ashes Tests for the Kangaroos off the bench late last season, and remains a big part of coach Kevin Walters’ plans for the World Cup in October and November. Keaon Koloamatangi is weighing up whether to skip the World Cup to undergo off-season surgery. Getty Images Koloamatangi’s ability to play on an edge as well as in the middle has not been lost on Walters, whose incumbent back-rowers Angus Crichton (rugby) and Hudson Young (Achilles) will be unavailable for the tournament on home soil. The 28-year-old Koloamatangi is also eligible to represent Tonga, and said the pay cut he would take to play for the Pacific nation – $850 match payments compared to a guaranteed $40,000 pay day representing Australia – was not a concern.



“When it comes to that [pay] stuff, we get paid pretty well with our salaries – if you only play for your country because of the money, that’s pretty weak,” Koloamatangi said. “My decision won’t be based on my money. My body is pretty sore at the moment, and I need to go for a few scans at the end of the year, just to see if I can play. “It’s a possibility [I don’t play at all]. I’ll keep it [my options] open. “I’ll get my knee checked out. I’ve also had a few niggles in the lower back, there’s been a bit of a disc issue.” Koloamatangi called coach Wayne Bennett on Christmas Eve to inform he had would take up a five-year, $5 million deal with the Dragons for the start of the 2027 season. Warriors playmaker Luke Metcalf, Titans winger Phil Sami, Roosters utility Connor Watson, Dolphins playmaker Kodi Nikorima and Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater have all committed to the Red V since then.



Related Article NRL 2026 The doctor who helped the one player return from a pec injury without surgery is backing Isaah Yeo Koloamatangi said he did not want any lingering injuries to prevent him from playing at his best at the World Cup. “I don’t want to make myself look like a fool if I don’t play well because I’m injured – I’ll make the call when the time comes,” Koloamatangi said. Koloamatangi will relish the forwards battle against Canterbury on Friday night. He injured his knee the last time the two clubs met on Good Friday, but Koloamatangi indicated after that game he had been nursing a PCL issue. World.title: ‘Devil will be in the detail’: Labor under pressure to unmask accused criminals
World.content:
Updated PoliticsVictoriaCourts ‘Devil will be in the detail’: Labor under pressure to unmask accused criminals Kieran Rooney and Erin Pearson Updated August 11, 2026 — 6:03pm ,first published 11:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Convicted rapists would no longer be able to hide their identity through suppression orders designed to protect victims if Labor is re-elected in November, a move welcomed by open justice advocates who nonetheless say broader reforms are required. The state government’s change – to be legislated after the election – represents a first step towards addressing concerns with suppression orders raised by media groups and highlighted by multiple high-profile cases in which alleged abusers have succeeded in remaining unnamed on mental health grounds. Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny and Premier Ben Carroll on Tuesday. AAP Premier Ben Carroll and Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny announced the commitment on Tuesday as they introduced legislation aimed at protecting victims of abuse, including restrictions on character references and a new standalone offence for coercive control. Carroll said Labor would amend the Open Courts Act to limit the use of suppression orders in the next term of parliament. As well as barring convicted rapists from using legal manoeuvres to hide their identities, the government also flagged it could wind back the use of suppression orders for those facing criminal trials, amid an ongoing review into the use of suppression orders.



Related Article Exclusive

Press freedom Court secrecy rules to be reviewed over suppression order complaints The Age revealed in June that Kilkenny had tasked the Department of Justice and Community Safety with this review work and to consult the courts, lawyers and the media. Limiting suppression orders for convicted rapists represents a fraction of the problem. Many of the high-profile cases that have shown flaws in the system – including Ralph Carr and Tom Silvagni – have used secrecy provisions to protect the identity of those on trial. Justin Quill, partner at top-tier law firm Thomsons, said the system was broken and reforms were a “no-brainer”. “The devil will be in the detail, and until we see that detail, it’s hard to know whether the government’s announced commitment is a real one or just one that’s being said for political purposes ahead of an election in November,” he said.



Quill said convicted offenders were not the key issue, and the biggest problem with the current system was the secrecy orders that could last for years while court proceedings were under way. “We’ve got to have openness and transparency in our judicial system from start to finish, not just after someone is convicted,” he said. Lawyers regularly rely on a clause in the Open Courts Act which allows suppression orders to be considered “to protect the safety of any person”, and the government is under pressure to address this element of the legislation. The use of mental health grounds under this clause to secure suppression orders has come under increased scrutiny in recent years, particularly after being used in the 2025 rape trial of Silvagni, a member of a famous footballing family.



Silvagni’s name was suppressed during criminal proceedings after a judge accepted publicity about his case would risk harming his mental health. Major media groups, including The Age, campaigned in March alongside victims of crime to change current legislation to make it harder to obtain suppression orders on mental health grounds. Kilkenny on Tuesday said the review would aim to close any loopholes being exploited. “Justice must be open, and there must be a balance with the right to a fair trial,” she said. “But we have seen most recently that we need to look at this. We need to listen.” The Coalition, if elected, has already vowed to restrict suppression orders to genuine physical safety reasons.



Melbourne Press Club president Michael Bachelard, who is also a journalist for The Age, said the government’s announcement was welcomed but limited and light on detail. Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted “The government and opposition should commit before the election to a much broader review into the law governing cases in Victoria, including the test that must be met before a suppression order is granted,” he said. “As they stand, these laws make it far too difficult in this state to keep the public informed.” For three years, Carr, 66, was on bail while he fought allegations that he raped a young woman at his Melbourne home. But the music producer did so under the cloak of anonymity. This was thanks to a wide-ranging suppression order that banned media from reporting his name, age and the industry he worked in, and from publishing pixelated photographs.



Even after a jury found him guilty of rape and sexual assault, he persisted with his suppression fight, arguing his psychological safety would be at significant risk if “public identification” occurred, before abandoning it last week. In June, this masthead revealed almost 500 suppression orders in various forms were issued in Victorian courts last year, with the highest number being issued on safety grounds – including for mental health reasons. Of those granted, 247 were made in the County Court. Last week, this masthead unmasked the identity of a doctor accused of filming women and children using showers at Melbourne public pools after fighting a suppression order sought on psychological safety grounds for the accused man’s son. He was granted a three-month interim suppression order to give lawyers time to gather evidence, despite the legislation stating these types of applications must be brought back before the court for determination as a “matter of urgency”. Melbourne University academic and lawyer Jason Bosland said: “Suppression orders that are made in circumstances that do not meet community expectations have a corrosive effect on such confidence and ultimately undermine the rule of law.”



The Carroll government also introduced a bill to parliament on Tuesday with a range of protections for victims of abuse. It included the introduction of coercive control as a standalone criminal offence, delivering on a commitment from 2025, and the removal of “good character” references which can be used to argue for lighter sentences. Harrison James has welcomed the abolition of good character references in Victoria. Riccardo Raiti Harrison James, a survivor of child sexual abuse and co-founder of the “Your Reference Ain’t Relevant” advocacy group, said character references had already been abolished in the ACT and NSW. “Good character is the very tool perpetrators use to ingratiate themselves into the lives of their victims, their families and their communities,” he said.



Related Article Justice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused “When we allow them to use that to reduce their sentence, we risk giving an offender a discount for the very thing that helped facilitate the crime.” The standalone offence of coercive control will take effect in March 2028 to provide time for an advisory group to consult on how it will be implemented. Katie Alexander, a member of the state’s Victim Survivors’ Advisory Council, said the area was so complex that a one-size-fits-all approach would not work. She said coercive control devastated her life and destroyed her family.



“It messed with my mind. It broke my body and it shattered my relationships,” Alexander said. “Repeated acts of abuse over many years have deep psychological, emotional, social and financial scars.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said her first act as Coalition leader had been to move legislation on coercive control, which was not supported by Labor at the time. “Coercive control is an insidious form of abuse and can affect anyone, but we know women are overwhelmingly the victims of intimate partner violence,” she said. “Protecting women and victim-survivors from abuse should never be political. We will always stand on the side of victim-survivors.” Other protections to be introduced include amendments to family violence intervention orders that reduce the need for victims to return to court for extensions and requiring courts to consider their views when making decisions on these extensions.



Personal safety intervention orders will also recognise grooming for the first time and fine exemptions will be extended to stop fees and charges being weaponised against victims of abuse. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Price hopes Canterbury return can start Monte Veebee on road to riches
World.content:
There’s no shortage of lucrative options in the back of co-trainer Luke Price’s mind for consistent galloper Monte Veebee beyond his return in the Chase The Dream Handicap (1250m) at Canterbury today.

It’s been a case of musical trainers for the five-year-old, who started out with the Robert and Luke Price team at Kembla but switched to the Bjorn Baker stable for his last campaign where he recorded a first-up provincial win and four city placings before coming back home.

Trainer Luke Price saddles up Monte Veebee at Canterbury on Wednesday evening. Getty Images

Price feels Monte Veebee could be an ideal horse to aim at the rich Provincial-Midway Championships series in the autumn, with its $1 million final, given he is eligible having come back to their stable well before the cut-off.

“He could be a good Four Pillars horse, too, but I hope his benchmark goes beyond that,” Price said. “I think we’ve got a city class horse back. It’s a good starting point and let’s hope he can start off like he did last prep.”

Selections based on a good to soft track. Race 1 2. Lorax put the writing on the wall with a strong first-up placing at Randwick, hitting the line from near last into third. Threads was placed in the Black Opal earlier in the year, he may have been in need of the run when fourth behind Sequinned two weeks ago. Open to improvement. 7. How to play it: Lorax WIN. Racing returns to Canterbury on Wednesday. Getty Images Race 2



2. Sing Your Song showed a lot of promise on debut back in April running on from well back into second behind Moscatel at 1100m. Nothing wrong with her two trials leading in, somewhat typical for the stable, she’s drawn to have every chance first-up. 1. World.title: Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis
World.content:
RBA governor Michele Bullock has warned the bank is willing to keep raising interest rates to curb inflation while flagging property prices could fall by 20 per cent without seriously risking the country’s financial stability. The decision followed a warning from ANZ economists that property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes. House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao In a press conference on Tuesday, Bullock said the downturn in the property market was “not a massive risk” to financial stability, not a major factor keeping interest rates on hold, and “not [currently] the main game” for the bank. “We’ve done a little bit of work on [the property market] from a financial stability perspective,” she said. “If property prices fell by 20 per cent, still only about 5 per cent of households would be in negative equity.



“Awful circumstances [for the homeowners affected], which are compounded by the fact that you’d have to sell your house, but it doesn’t pose a risk to the financial institutions because they are very well capitalised.” On Tuesday, the bank kept the official cash rate on hold at 4.35 per cent – the same rate it set for all of 2024 – while releasing updated forecasts that showed inflation staying above the 2 to 3 per cent target band until the end of 2027. Financial markets believe there is a 50-50 chance of a further rate rise late in the year, with rate relief not expected before the second half of 2027. Bullock said the decision to keep interest rates on hold was unanimous, that a rate cut was not discussed, and that the board remained focused on ensuring high inflation did not become entrenched.



“We’ve already raised [rates] three times, and we will go again if we need to,” Bullock said. “I think personally that it’s quite possible we might need to go, but we’ll wait and see what the data tells us. Editor's pick Census Completing the census is compulsory. Skipping it can result in a hefty fine The board said in its report: “Following three increases in the cash-rate target since the beginning of the year, financial conditions are now tighter than they were, and the economy appears to be slowing as expected … But inflation is still too high.” Inflation is likely to remain high for some time, the bank warned, because of the disruption to global oil supply caused by the Iran war that meant higher fuel prices were flowing through to other goods and services. Bullock also said there was a risk that the AI-driven data centre boom in Australia could put pressure on areas such as construction, which is already facing high demand, possibly keeping inflation elevated before the nation sees any productivity improvements from the technology.



The bank said while household consumption had eased gradually, business investment had been much stronger than expected, largely driven by data centre construction. The board “will still need to see some further progress before [it] can be confident that we are going to get inflation back to target with current monetary policy settings,” Bullock said. Loading The bank’s latest forecasts show it expects economic growth to be slightly stronger, though still lacklustre, for the rest of the year compared to its forecasts in May, coming in at 1.4 per cent by Christmas and 1.6 per cent by December next year. Price growth across the economy remains above the RBA’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent, at 3.8 per cent in June, but the inflation figures were substantially lower than the 4.8 per cent figure the RBA forecast in May.



Unemployment, at 4.4 per cent in June, is still outside the rate the bank considers “full employment”. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow Treasurer Jim Chalmers told parliament the Reserve Bank’s decision to keep interest rates steady would “come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage”. “This decision reflects the fact that inflation has been coming in well under the Reserve Bank and Treasury forecasts,” Chalmers said. Earlier on Tuesday, ANZ said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year.



Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough. Related Article Exclusive

Property prices Teal MPs’ electorates are where house values are falling most. They think it’s a good thing The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak. Prices in both cities are expected to recover by almost 5 per cent in 2028. ANZ senior economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said the market was slowing sooner than they had expected due to a combination of restrictive interest rates, tax policy changes and global uncertainty. “Auction clearance rates are very soft, coming in below 50 per cent for the past 10 weeks across the capitals,” they said. World.title: RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalInterest rates RBA’s threat of a rate rise rings a bit hollow Shane Wright August 11, 2026 — 5:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Reserve Bank is making a lot of noise that it could lift interest rates. But the RBA’s own forecasts and analysis suggest that barring another unexpected inflation spike – the world’s looking at you, Donald Trump – it is going to struggle to follow through with that threat. RBA governor Michele Bullock on Tuesday. Brent Lewin While governor Michele Bullock often says the Reserve only has one lever to deal with inflation, she actually has another. And she deploys it every time she stands up to do a press conference or make public statements. Her voice is a powerful one. If she were to warn of economic disaster or bright days ahead, consumers, investors and markets would listen and act. In central bank jargon, it’s called jawboning.



And threatening to inflict more interest pain on the economy is a good example of jawboning. Again and again on Tuesday, she said there were upside risks to inflation and that the bank may have to tighten monetary policy further. But compare her words with the bank’s forecasts released with the decision to leave the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent. Loading The bank thinks inflation is going to be lower than it had expected. Unemployment is going to be a tad higher than it had forecast. Wages growth is a little softer. That’s all before the RBA gets a firm grip on what its previous rate rises and the federal government’s changes to property taxes – and the fallout from higher oil prices on consumer sentiment – are doing to house prices.



As the bank knows, house prices are a key swing factor in the strength of consumer spending. “Lower housing prices weigh on household consumption by reducing household net wealth and spending related to housing turnover. Weaker housing prices also reduce the incentive to build new homes,” it said. Where do the bank’s biggest inflationary threats lie? In household spending and in housing construction costs. The bank sliced its household spending forecasts, and it really cut its expectations for housing investment. In May, it thought spending on new homes would have grown by 2 per cent by year’s end. Now it thinks it’s going to contract by 0.7 per cent. Good luck to builders trying to pass on higher costs to prospective home owners when the RBA thinks there will be fewer of them.



The rates decision was announced as ANZ went the full bear on the Australian property market, predicting a peak to trough in housing prices of more than 10 per cent. In Sydney, the nation’s capital when it comes to property fascination and prices, the drop is tipped to be closer to 15 per cent. Related Article Updated

Property prices Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis Bullock finished her press conference by saying if the bank believed it would be wrong on its inflation forecasts, then it would act. As the great central banker of Springfield, Homer Simpson, would say: D’oh! Analysts assumed she was talking about its inflation forecasts being too dovish. But the bank got its last inflation forecast wrong. Instead of it being 4.8 per cent to June, it was 3.8 per cent.



Missed it by the side of a barn, really. There were good reasons for the miss – petrol prices have not soared nearly as high as feared – but it was still a long way out. And it missed its underlying inflation forecast. And it missed its unemployment forecast. And it downgraded its wage growth forecast. There’s nothing wrong with Bullock using her central bank pulpit to talk up the threat of a rate rise. It’s an important part of her armoury and one that has been tried and tested. In some ways, it can work better than a rate rise, without some of the collateral economic damage. But with previous rate rises still yet to fully work their way through the economy, and the federal government’s property tax changes taking the wind out of the national housing Ponzi scheme, something from left field will have to emerge to force Bullock to follow through with her threat. World.title: ‘Like he’d seen a ghost’: Ex-girlfriend says former teen athlete confided in her about Alan Jones
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former teen athlete who was allegedly indecently assaulted by Alan Jones looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he confided in his then girlfriend that the veteran broadcaster had been touching him inappropriately, a court has heard. The ex-girlfriend of complainant “J”, one of six men who has accused Jones of unwanted kissing and touching, told Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial on Tuesday that “J” swore her to secrecy after telling her about the alleged assaults. Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy “He was really uncomfortable with telling me. He had his head down,” she said.



“He did sort of aggressively [say], ‘you cannot tell anybody about this’. It was, ‘you can’t repeat it’ or, ‘you’ve got to keep it to yourself’, it was along the lines of that.” She told the Downing Centre Local Court that “J” made the disclosure during a late-night conversation in her parents’ loungeroom in the mid-2000s. He had arrived from Jones’ southern NSW property looking “emotionless” and like he had “seen a ghost”, she said. “I remember his face very clearly in my mind, and it still is very clear in my mind,” she said. He told her that “Alan Jones has touched me inappropriately”, she said.



She said “J” was not his normal self and was not looking her in the eye. She suggested to him that “maybe you want to report it” and he responded firmly, “No”, she told the court. ‘Tell my truth’ Years later, after Jones was arrested in 2024, she said “J” contacted her by text message, and they spoke later that night. “J” told her that “I’d like to come forward and tell my truth”, she said. She responded that she thought this was important, the court heard, and that “I remember you telling me all those years ago”. Complainant “J” was the first witness to give evidence in the former broadcaster’s lengthy criminal trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent.



Related Article Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial as it happened: Court hears brother of complainant ‘J’ received gifts from 2GB broadcaster as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues He alleges Jones kissed him and touched his penis without his consent. On the Crown’s case, the alleged assaults took place in the early 2000s when “J” was aged between 17 and 19. The former broadcaster vehemently denies wrongdoing and is defending the charges. Of the 22 charges, nine counts of indecent assault relate to “J”, who completed his evidence on Tuesday. A further five complainants will give evidence in the trial. Jones’ gifts to family of ‘J’



The brother of complainant “J” told the court on Tuesday that the then broadcaster had not only given his brother a series of gifts but had also bought him expensive presents. He said “J” had told him that “Alan would like to help out” with an engagement ring when he was planning to propose to his now wife. Jones had also bought the couple a Villeroy & Boch dinner set as a wedding gift, “J”’s brother told the court. Under cross-examination by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, he said he did not recall other gifts, after Bashir asked about a dishwasher for the family home, flowers for their mother and hampers. The brother of “J” said he was aware that Jones had given his brother a series of gifts including a mobile phone, a car, and a weekly allowance of hundreds of dollars. Records tendered in court suggest “J” received the phone about a month after his 18th birthday and the car when he was 19.



The brother told the court that “J” confided in him about the alleged indecent assaults after Jones’ arrest in November 2024. “J” had asked to meet him at a nearby McDonald’s, he told the court, and had said: “This is the hardest thing that I’ve ever had to tell you. You’ve probably seen the news about the defendant. “I’m one of the people who has come forward.” He said he asked “J” why he hadn’t told him earlier and “J” had replied that it was hard for him and he didn’t know what to do. “J” said he didn’t want “the money, the support” from Jones to stop, his brother said. He said he asked “J” how bad it had been and “J” had replied: “Nothing too bad. He didn’t try to f--- me or anything like that. He would try, he would grab me on the c---, he would kiss me … the hugs would go for longer.”



Related Article Analysis

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones’ front-row view as graphic details of alleged indecent assault are exposed Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, if he had witnessed Jones act inappropriately towards “J”, his brother said: “I didn’t.” Earlier on Tuesday, “J” was asked about texts with his former partner as he was re-examined by Wright during his sixth day of evidence. The complainant had told the court he confided in his then-girlfriend about the allegations. Last week, “J” was taken to texts exchanged with the woman after she went to police to make a statement while detectives were investigating accusations related to “J”. In those 2024 texts, he told the woman he would look after her “after it is all over”, referring to the court proceedings. Bashir suggested he was referring to financial support.



The woman wrote that speaking to police “brought back a lot” and that she didn’t remember some of it. “J” responded: “That’s great news, thank you. I didn’t want to discuss anything, so everything was all from what you remembered. I appreciate you meeting with him and providing a statement.” “J” wrote that when it was “all over” they could meet up, and he could tell her his story. The complainant denied he was alluding to financial support when he said he’d look after her, saying he was talking about her difficult sobriety journey. “I anticipated she’d have to go to court … I was grateful if she’d remembered anything,” he said.



“I was just going to support her to do that for me.” The man was also asked during re-examination by Wright why he had lied to his mother when he spoke with her following media coverage of the allegations against Jones in late 2023. The court heard he told her Jones had never touched him. He said he felt that she would have pushed him to come forward to police if he had told her. “I thought I would be called a liar and crushed in court and no one would believe me,” he said. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Labor MP took donations from club with pokies, reports himself to watchdog
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWPolitical donations Labor MP took donations from club with pokies, reports himself to watchdog Patrick Begley August 11, 2026 — 5:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A NSW Labor politician accepted thousands of dollars from a club with poker machines after the Minns government banned political donations from clubs involved in gambling. Records show Campbelltown MP Greg Warren received donations from the NSW Harness Racing Club in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Campbelltown MP Greg Warren said the harness racing club had declared it was not a prohibited donor. Greg Warren MP website The payments were made at fundraising lunch events hosted for Warren, which have featured Premier Chris Minns and Treasurer Daniel Mookhey. Following questions from this masthead, Warren said he had accepted the money “in good faith” but he would refer the payments to the electoral watchdog for assessment.



NSW, which has more poker machines than any other state or territory, closed a donations law “loophole” in 2023 by expanding the definition of gambling entity to include not-for-profit clubs with an involvement in gambling. “It is common sense,” Minns said at the time. “If other gambling entities are banned from making political donations, it should apply to all clubs.” Soon after the ban took effect, Warren held a corporate lunch attended by Minns at which the NSW Harness Racing Club contributed $3000, electoral records show. The NSW government closed a “loophole” in 2023 by banning not-for-profit clubs involved in gambling from making political donations. Peter Braig Warren recorded a $1500 donation from the club at a “Daniel Mookhey lunch” in 2024 and a further $1500 last year.



Trading as Club Menangle, the organisation operates a major racetrack south-west of Sydney, “home to the iconic Miracle Mile and the world’s richest harness race, The TAB Eureka”. It also runs the Menangle Country Club, which boasts an award-winning restaurant, picturesque garden and historic setting. Related Article Poker machines Second mega-club in firing line over dirty cash claims The venues have 50 poker machines, according to the most recent state records. Each year, the club’s accounts record poker machine revenue and commissions received from Keno and TAB sales. But most revenue comes from “TAB and wagering distributions” received from betting operators for putting on the race events. Registered clubs are banned from making political donations “if the business undertaken by the registered club includes wagering, betting, or other gambling”. It is a criminal offence to knowingly receive a prohibited donation.



Warren said the club had declared it was not prohibited. The Menangle Country Club, one of the venues operated by the NSW Harness Racing Club. Menangle Country Club “The donations were accepted in good faith with the required non-prohibited donor declaration, and were fully disclosed as per the required rules,” Warren said in a statement. “I take the required obligations under the Electoral Funding Act seriously, and have therefore taken the appropriate action for the donations to be referred to the NSW Electoral Commission for review.” Club chief executive Bruce Christison was unavailable to answer questions for medical reasons, a club spokeswoman said.



“The club has completed the political donations questionnaires honestly and transparently,” the spokeswoman said. Related Article Exclusive

Poker machines The battle over pokies comes to premier’s backyard “To ensure there is not an issue with our eligibility, we have contacted the electoral commission this morning and supplied all the relevant details and are now awaiting their response.” The NSW Electoral Commission declined to answer detailed questions, including whether the NSW Harness Racing Club met the definition of prohibited donor. The premier has faced significant pressure from within his own party to curb the problem gambling harm caused by poker machines, this masthead revealed in May.



On Monday, Minns told the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing that the government was considering pokies reforms ahead of the next election, saying “it’s clearly doing harm in the community”. A report by the NSW Audit Office last year found the regulation of pokies was “not supporting harm minimisation outcomes effectively”.
